title: Leila George Lands Lead Role Opposite Miles Teller In Black Label Thriller ‘Copperhead’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Leila George, the Australian-American actress known for turns in the likes of Disclaimer and Love Story, is set for a lead role opposite Miles Teller in Copperhead, the thriller from Black Label Media that shoots this month. Details as to the part are being kept under wraps, though sources said the character name is Leah. George joins a stacked […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Leila George, the Australian-American actress known for turns in the likes of Disclaimer and Love Story, is set for a lead role opposite Miles Teller in Copperhead, the thriller from Black Label Media that shoots this month.

Details as to the part are being kept under wraps, though sources said the character name is Leah. George joins a stacked cast also including Jason Momoa, Tenoch Huerta, Adria Arjona and Kiefer Sutherland.

Directed by Venice prize-winner John Swab, Copperhead‘s plot is thrust into motion when an undercover drug deal explodes into violence. A veteran detective is then forced to team with a young federal agent to unravel the conspiracy within their elite task force.

The film, penned by Chad Feehan and J. Todd Scott, is up for sales at TIFF via Black Bear. Black Label Media financed the project and is producing alongside Teller’s Lime Tree Productions and Swab’s Milk Boy, with CAA Media Finance and WME Independent co-repping domestic rights.

Watch on Deadline

Breaking out with a role in Alfonso Cuarón’s Apple TV+ limited series Disclaimer, which earned her a Critics Choice Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress, George has most recently been seen in Ryan Murphy’s Love Story for FX, where she played Kelly Klein — photographer and one-time wife of fashion designer Calvin Klein — as well as Netflix’s Emmy-winning limited series The Beast in Me.

Previously, George was a series regular on TNT’s Animal Kingdom, appearing across three seasons. She stars opposite Jake Gyllenhaal in Amazon MGM’s Road House 2 and will also be seen coming up in Netflix/Amblin’s series All the Sinners Bleed, as well as Oliver Stone’s White Lies, opposite Josh Hartnett. She is repped by WME, Strand Entertainment, United Agents, and United Management.

title: Annie Gonzalez Nabs Lead Role In Vanessa Guillén Biopic
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Annie Gonzalez (Flamin’ Hot, Jenni) has been set as the lead in the upcoming Vanessa Guillén biopic from Jolene Rodriguez and Jorge Xolalpa of Mighty Aphrodite Pictures. Gonzalez will play Mayra Guillén, the slain U.S. Army Specialist’s older sister, who has also signed on to the project as an executive producer. The as-yet-untitled narrative feature drama […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Annie Gonzalez (Flamin’ Hot, Jenni) has been set as the lead in the upcoming Vanessa Guillén biopic from Jolene Rodriguez and Jorge Xolalpa of Mighty Aphrodite Pictures.

Gonzalez will play Mayra Guillén, the slain U.S. Army Specialist’s older sister, who has also signed on to the project as an executive producer. The as-yet-untitled narrative feature drama will tell Vanessa Guillén’s story from the point of view of Mayra Guillén.

Developed in collaboration with the Guillén family, the project will chronicle the life of the young Army recruit whose 2020 disappearance and murder at Fort Hood in Texas sparked a nationwide outcry and calls for reform within the U.S. military.

Guillén had long had the goal of serving in the Army but, after being assigned to Fort Hood, told friends and family of being sexually harassed by a superior. She did not report it officially for fear of retaliation. She was later bludgeoned to death by fellow soldier Aaron David Robinson. Guillén had been missing for more than two months before some of her remains were found buried along the Leon River. Robinson fled Fort Hood after learning of the discovery. When law enforcement tried to apprehend him, he fatally shot himself.

Watch on Deadline

The film seeks to celebrate Guillén’s life while honoring the tireless advocacy of her family, whose campaigning inspired lasting legislative change and amplified the voices of military families.

Rodriguez and Xolalpa serve as the film’s producers. In addition to Mayra Guillén, Natalie Khawam and Alejandra Palomera also executive produce.

The production team is currently in the process of identifying a director to lead the project. Further announcements regarding the creative team and additional casting will be shared as the film moves through its development phase.

Gonzalez is no stranger to leading biopics about powerful women. In 2023, she executive produced and starred as Mexican singer Jenni Rivera, known by her fans as “La Diva De La Banda,” in the ViX film Jenni. She also portrayed Judy Montañez, wife of Richard Montañez, who, it has been claimed, invented Flamin’ Hot Cheetos in the lauded Eva Longoria-directed Flamin’ Hot (2023). Most recently, she was featured in the ensemble cast of the Amazon MGM Studios Original film Relationship Goals, directed by Linda Mendoza and led by Kelly Rowland and Cliff “Method Man” Smith. Up next, Gonzalez will star in Wild Ones, from first-time feature filmmaker Manuel Figueroa. She is repped by Innovative Artists and Granderson Des Rochers.

title: Danielle Deadwyler, Ella Beatty, Ike Barinholtz, Connor Storrie & More Confirmed For Focus Features’ ‘The Bell Jar’ As Production Wraps
summary: Focus Features has wrapped production on its adaptation of the classic Sylvia Plath novel The Bell Jar, starring Billie Eilish and Carey Mulligan, confirming the supporting cast, which includes Danielle Deadwyler (Till), Dylan Hawco (Ice Cream Man), Lili Taylor (Daredevil: Born Again), Ella Beatty (Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story), Maggie Kuntz (Broadway’s John Proctor Is the Villain), […]
content:
Focus Features has wrapped production on its adaptation of the classic Sylvia Plath novel The Bell Jar, starring Billie Eilish and Carey Mulligan, confirming the supporting cast, which includes Danielle Deadwyler (Till), Dylan Hawco (Ice Cream Man), Lili Taylor (Daredevil: Born Again), Ella Beatty (Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story), Maggie Kuntz (Broadway’s John Proctor Is the Villain), Ike Barinholtz (The Studio), and Connor Storrie (Heated Rivalry).

We previously reported on Beatty being in final talks; Storrie had been heavily rumored as part of the cast.

The only novel penned by American writer and poet Plath, The Bell Jar is a semi-autobiographical work charting a young woman’s descent into mental illness and the burden of societal pressures. Originally published in 1963, the book paralleled Plath’s own experiences with depression; the writer tragically died by suicide just a month after the novel’s first UK publication. In the U.S., the book became an instant bestseller, and has since been translated into more than 40 languages, with millions of copies sold worldwide.

Watch on Deadline

The Bell Jar marks 10-time Grammy winner Eilish’s feature acting debut. She plays the lead role of Esther Greenwood, with Mulligan as Mrs. Greenwood, Deadwyler as Dr. Nolan, Hawco as Buddy Willard, Taylor as Jay Cee, Beatty as Joan, Kuntz as Doreen, Barinholtz as Lenny, and Storrie as Marco.

Sarah Polley directs from her own adapted screenplay, in her first feature outing since winning the Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay for Women Talking in 2023. The film is produced by Plan B, Studiocanal and Joy Coalition.

Polley is represented by WME, GGA, and Circle Management + Production; Eilish by WME, Sandbox Entertainment, and Gang, Tyre, Ramer; Mulligan by Julian Belfrage, CAA, and Jackoway Austen; Deadwyler by Paradigm, Play Management, and Ziffren Brittenham; Barinholtz by UTA, Artists First, and Jared Levine of Yorn, Levine, Barnes; Hawco by GGA, Gersh and Circle Management + Production; Taylor by Independent Artist Group, Untitled Entertainment, and Schreck Rose Dapello; Beatty by Entertainment 360 and CAA; Kuntz by Verve and The Rozenzweig Group; and Storrie by CAA, Atlas Artists, Linden Entertainment and Yorn Levine.

title: Miramax Developing Film Adaptation Of Alloy Romantic Thriller Novel ‘Everything We Never Said’; Amy Andelson & Emily Meyer Scripting
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Miramax is developing a feature adaptation of Everything We Never Said, Alloy Entertainment’s YA romantic thriller novel from Sloan Harlow, with Amy Andelson and Emily Meyer aboard to adapt the screenplay. Published by G.P. Putnam’s Sons in 2024, Everything We Never Said follows Ella Graham, who, in the wake of her best friend Hayley’s death, finds herself falling […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Miramax is developing a feature adaptation of Everything We Never Said, Alloy Entertainment‘s YA romantic thriller novel from Sloan Harlow, with Amy Andelson and Emily Meyer aboard to adapt the screenplay.

Published by G.P. Putnam’s Sons in 2024, Everything We Never Said follows Ella Graham, who, in the wake of her best friend Hayley’s death, finds herself falling for Hayley’s boyfriend, Sawyer. But when Ella sorts through her late friend’s belongings and uncovers her diary, she’s rattled by the secrets Hayley kept and learns she might be walking into something much darker than she realized.

Harlow’s novel lit up BookTok, making bestseller lists from both the New York Times and USA Today, and being named a Barnes & Noble Young Adult Book of the Month. Alloy’s president and chief creative officer, Leslie Morgenstein, and executive vice president of theatrical film production, Elysa Koplovitz Dutton, will produce the feature take. Arianna D’Andrea is overseeing the project for Miramax.

Watch on Deadline

Everything We Never Said was developed by Alloy Entertainment’s New York-based book division, then licensed to G.P. Putnam’s Sons for publishing, with Alloy retaining film & TV rights. This is the same model Alloy has employed for hit series including The Vampire Diaries, Netflix’s You, Gossip Girl and the Pretty Little Liars franchise, and films including the Adam Sandler-produced You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah.

Andelson and Meyer are the writers and creators of the Netflix series Trinkets, which won three Emmy Awards for Best Young Adult Program and Best Writing for a Children/Young Adult Program. Previously, they adapted F. Scott Fitzgerald’s classic The Great Gatsby for 20th and director Jon M. Chu. Additionally, they wrote the screenplays for Chu’s Step Up 3D, as well as the romantic dramedy Naomi and Ely’s No Kiss List, directed by Kristin Hanggi and starring Victoria Justice and Pierson Fodé. Their YA novel Layover was released in 2018, after being sold in a bidding war to Random House. They are repped by Artists First and Goodman, Genow, Schenkman.

title: ‘The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon’ Final Season Reveals First-Look Teaser (TV News Roundup)
summary: AMC+ revealed the first look for the fourth and final season of “The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon.” The final season premieres in 2027. Daryl Dixon’s journey, which began in 2010, is finally coming to an end in the concluding season of the series, a spinoff from the original “Walking Dead” series. The new season sees […]
content:
AMC+ revealed the first look for the fourth and final season of “The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon.” The final season premieres in 2027.

Daryl Dixon’s journey, which began in 2010, is finally coming to an end in the concluding season of the series, a spinoff from the original “Walking Dead” series. The new season sees Daryl (Norman Reedus) and Carol (Melissa McBride) cross the badlands of Spain. They are joined by Captain Alejandro Perkins (Jimmy Smits), a former U.S. Navy officer and medical doctor who found a unique way to survive during the apocalypse.

Also starring are Romain Levi, Eduardo Noriega, Óscar Jaenada, Candela Saitta and Hugo Arbués.

Popular on Variety

The series is executive produced by showrunner David Zabel, Scott M. Gimple, Reedus, McBride, Greg Nicotero, Brian Bockrath, Angela Kang, Jason Richman, Dan Percival and Steve Squillante.

The spinoff series launched in 2023, following Daryl on an unexpected journey across Europe. Along with its sister spinoff “The Walking Dead: Dead City,” the series has continued the franchise since the original show’s conclusion in 2022 after 11 seasons.

See the teaser trailer below.

Also in this week’s TV News Roundup:

CASTING

Alvina August has joined the cast of “The Rookie” spinoff series, “The Rookie: North.”

August joins previously announced cast members Jay Ellis, Chris Sullivan, Froy Gutierrez, Karen Fukuhara, Mya Lowe, Janet Montgomery and Malik Watson. No details of August’s character have been revealed.

The spinoff follows Alex Holland (Ellis), who, after a violent home invasion, faces a midlife crisis that forces him to confront a lifetime of his shortcomings. His solution? Join the Pierce County Police Department in Washington as its oldest rookie.

August recently starred in Season 3 of “Invasion,” as well as “Nancy Drew” and “Lucky Hank” alongside Bob Odenkirk. Her additional credits include “Chilling Adventures of Sabrina,” “The Boys,” “The Good Doctor,” “Suits” and “Supernatural.” August is represented by Buchwald and Performers Management.

*

Ana Brenda Contreras and Erick Elías will lead the cast of “Emergencias. Unidad de Vida,” a new Telemundo medical drama.

The series follows Gabriela Serrano, who is an ambitiously talented medical resident returning to her hometown, where she must confront her family’s complicated past while navigating a hospital that’s future isn’t guaranteed.

Joining Contreras and Elías are Geraldine Bazán, Ana Belena, Rodolfo Salas, Elizabeth Gutiérrez, Laura Flores, Mónica Dionne, David Palacio and Luis Ernesto Franco. The series also features Gloria Aura, Jerónimo Cantillo, Elena Medina, Miguel Ferreira, Paola Fernández, Pepe Gámez, Vince Miranda, Roberto Mateos, Gloria Peralta, Emma Ramos, Sebastián Silva, Johann Vera and Sara Linares. Arturo Peniche will also make a special appearance.

“Emergencias. Unidad de Vida” has officially begun production in Miami. The series is a Telemundo Studios production written by Carlos Eloy Castro and directed by Nicolas Di Blasi and Luis Sierra, with Javier Pons, Jacky Castro and Martha Godoy as executive producers.

FIRST LOOKS

Prime Video released the first official images of “Boys of Tommen” at the two-day Obsessed Retreat: Class of ’26 event in The Alps, Germany.

The romantic drama series based on the New York Times bestselling series by Chloe Walsh stars Nancy Surridge as Shannon Lynch, Conor Sánchez as Johnny Kavanagh, James O’Donoghue as Joey Lynch and Sophie McGibbon as Aoife Molloy.

The official logline reads: “‘Boys of Tommen’ follows the forbidden love story of Johnny Kavanagh, the star rugby player on the verge of a pro career, and Shannon Lynch, the talented but painfully shy new girl at the prestigious private school of Tommen College in Ballylaggin, Ireland. Both teenagers are hiding secrets; Johnny, a potentially career-ending injury, and Shannon, a troubled and violent homelife. Through their secret and highly charged connection, the two teens from opposite worlds battle against the odds and find a way to save each other.”

The series is produced by global independent studio Wiip in association with Amazon MGM Studios, with Metropolitan providing local production services. Adapted by Poppy Cogan, Season One will be based on the first two novels in Walsh’s series, “Binding 13” and “Keeping 13.” Cogan serves as an executive producer alongside Walsh, Wiip’s Paul Lee, Hope Hartman and Sean Flanagan, Temple Hill’s Wyck Godfrey Marty Bowen, James Seidman and Annika Patton and Drama Republic’s Greg Brenman and Deena Butt. Carla Stronge serves as casting director. Brendan Canty (Christy) is directing the series, while Ingrid Goodwin serves as the series producer.

Christian Tierney/Prime

title: ‘Meta Labs’ Debut at Best Buy to Offer Free Demos of Tech Giant’s Latest AI Glasses and VR Headsets
summary: Meta is teaming up with Best Buy to offer fans of the brand and curious customers alike a chance to demo the new Meta product lineup up-close and in person. Select Best Buy locations across the country are now offering hands-on demos of the trendy Ray-Ban Meta and Oakley Meta glasses, the Meta Ray-Ban Display […]
content:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

is teaming up with Best Buy to offer fans of the brand and curious customers alike a chance to demo the new Meta product lineup up-close and in person.

Select Best Buy locations across the country are now offering hands-on demos of the trendy Ray-Ban Meta and Oakley Meta glasses, the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses and the popular Meta Quest VR headset, giving shoppers a chance to see how the products work in real-life settings.

“Meta Lab @ Best Buy” will offer demos of all the products, bringing the AI glasses and VR headsets to life through interactive displays and activations. Customers can try on the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses, for example, to read information right in front of their eyes from the lenses, and learn how to use hand gestures to swipe or tap without ever needing to take the phone out.

Popular on Variety

VR headsets like the Meta Quest 3 and Meta Quest 3S will also be available to demo, letting customers play their favorite games, try a workout or watch a movie in immersive 3D environments and stunning realism.

And of course, the popular Ray-Ban Meta and Oakley Meta glasses will be available to shop, with product specialists helping customers find a pair of frames to fit their face shape, personality and style. Meta sales specialists will also demo some of the new features of the smartglasses, which now go beyond just video recording to also provide improved music listening capabilities and live translation, among other features.

The first Meta Lab @ Best Buy “store in store” opened in June, with more rolling out throughout the summer. Meta says the experience will be available in more than 50 Best Buy locations across the US and Canada by the end of the year. See a full list of participation locations here.

title: Nick Offerman Slams Ben Shapiro’s ‘Rampant Homophobia’ After Being Attacked for Playing a Gay Role: ‘Holy S—. That’s Crazy’
summary: Nick Offerman recently appeared on the “Talk Easy With Sam Fragoso” podcast and blasted Ben Shapiro’s “rampant homophobia” after seeing a video for the first time of the Daily Wire co-founder and political commenter’s attacking Offerman’s gay role in HBO’s “The Last of Us.” “The entire episode has no zombies, no real threat, and it […]
content:
Nick Offerman recently appeared on the “Talk Easy With Sam Fragoso” podcast and blasted Ben Shapiro‘s “rampant homophobia” after seeing a video for the first time of the Daily Wire co-founder and political commenter’s attacking Offerman’s gay role in HBO’s “The Last of Us.”

“The entire episode has no zombies, no real threat, and it is about two gay dudes who meet and have a relationship, in which one grows strawberries for the other, and then they die,” Shapiro said, noting Offerman “likes to nail dudes” in the episode. “There’s gay Ron Swanson, and it’s complete with sex scenes and the whole thing. And gay Ron Swanson decides that he is also going to commit suicide at the same time because of ‘Romeo and Juliet,’ or ‘Romeo and Romeo’ in this particular case.”

“Holy shit… that’s crazy,” Offerman responded to the video. “That’s the most Ben Shapiro I’ve ever seen, and there’s a very good reason for that. I mean, I don’t know what to say. I’m embarrassed for his reading comprehension. I think he got eight things wrong in his recap, besides his rampant homophobia.”

Popular on Variety

Offerman starred opposite Murray Bartlett in “The Last of Us” episode “Long, Long Time,” which took a break from the main storyline of the show’s first season to spotlight the love story between two men over 20 years as the world succumbs to a zombie virus. The episode earned near universal acclaim from critics, but that didn’t stop homophobic trolls from taking issue with the show for spotlighting a gay romance.

In an interview with Variety earlier this year, Offerman said he tunes out toxic online backlash to his work because “you can’t navigate life steering by Twitter trolls, the sadness of Elon Musk and his minions,” adding: “I navigate my life by the writings of Wendell Berry and the values my mom and dad gave me. I willfully ignore the overall public zeitgeist. Something from this article might put me on some Ben Shapiro list, where a bunch of jerks literally will just call me ‘f****t’ or worse on my social media. It’s a pattern. It’s laughable and sad, but it’s also just humiliating.

Offerman won an Emmy and an Independent Spirit Award for his performance in “The Last of Us.” During his acceptance speech at the latter awards ceremony, he took aim at the toxic trolls outraged over his decision to play a gay character.

“Thanks to HBO for having the guts to participate in this storytelling tradition that is truly independent,” he said. “Stories with guts that when homophobic hate comes my way and says, ‘Why did you have to make it a gay story?’ We say, ‘Because you ask questions like that. It’s not a gay story it’s a love story, you asshole!”

Watch Offerman’s full interview on “Talk Easy with Sam Fragoso” in the video below.

title: Suno and Believe Music Announce Strategic Partnership
summary: Suno, the controversial AI music generating platform, continues to make moves toward legitimacy in the music industry: After striking licensing deals with Warner Music and BMG (arguably the third and fourth largest music companies in the world), on Tuesday it has announced a deal with France-based independent music company Believe. The deal also covers TuneCore, […]
content:
Suno, the controversial AI music generating platform, continues to make moves toward legitimacy in the music industry: After striking licensing deals with Warner Music and BMG (arguably the third and fourth largest music companies in the world), on Tuesday it has announced a deal with France-based independent music company Believe. The deal also covers TuneCore, Believe’s digital distribution division.

Under the agreement, music from participating Believe and TuneCore artists and labels will be included in the new music models that Suno is launching in partnership with the music industry, and artists and labels can choose to opt in to new, licensed music products that the companies will create together, the announcement states. Artists who consent to participate will be compensated for their music and their rights will be protected, it continues. They will also benefit from Suno’s training protections and recently announced transparency tools and download limits.

All tracks created by artists using Suno’s new industry partner model will become eligible to distribute through Believe and TuneCore. This change from Believe’s April 2026 decision to block the distribution of Suno’s then-current models reflects the progress achieved in recent months for artists.

Popular on Variety

“For 20 years, we have been helping artists and labels reach their full potential, and increasingly that means working with new technology like AI, while ensuring that responsible innovation translates into greater opportunities and value-generation for artists. The partnership we worked on with Suno for Believe and TuneCore unlocks powerful tools for all artists and labels. It now gives them a meaningful choice over how they can participate, protect their rights and enables them to share the value created by innovative responsible AI technologies”, said Denis Ladegaillerie, Founder and CEO of Believe.

“We have always shared a common goal with Believe to support independent artists at all stages of their careers. This partnership will significantly expand opportunities for independent artists, giving them access to creative tools, new paths to distribute their music through Believe and TuneCore, and more exposure”, said Mikey Shulman, CEO of Suno. “We’ve been laying the foundation for the next generation of Suno, strengthening our safeguards, expanding our industry partnerships, and learning from artists testing our upcoming music models. We’re thrilled to work with Believe on innovative product experiences that will give their artists new ways to earn and build even deeper connections with their fans.”

Suno, which has had a highly combative relationship with the music industry in recent years. Despite its licensing deals with Warner (which previously sued it) and recently BMG, it is in ongoing legal action with Universal and Sony over unauthorized use of their copyrighted material, and was sued earlier this week by Grammy-winning Americana singer Jason Isbell and others, who claim the company has allowed users to produce tracks based on musicians’ identities with its models without their consent. Last month a German court found that the company was violating U.S. and German copyright laws.

title: Jim Geoghan, ‘Suite Life of Zack & Cody’ Co-Creator, Dies at 79
summary: Jim Geoghan, the creator of “Suite Life of Zack & Cody,” died on Sept. 6 at 79 in Los Angeles, his daughter Genevieve Geoghan confirmed to Variety. He was 79. He co-created and executive produced “The Suite Life of Zack & Cody,” the Disney Channel sitcom that brought Cole and Dylan Sprouse, Ashley Tisdale, Brenda […]
content:
Jim Geoghan, the creator of “Suite Life of Zack & Cody,” died on Sept. 6 at 79 in Los Angeles, his daughter Genevieve Geoghan confirmed to Variety. He was 79.

He co-created and executive produced “The Suite Life of Zack & Cody,” the Disney Channel sitcom that brought Cole and Dylan Sprouse, Ashley Tisdale, Brenda Song and more to the spotlight. Following the Sprouse brothers as rebellious and playful tweens raised in a hotel, the series ran from 2005 to 2008 for three seasons before switching to the seas in “The Suite Life on Deck.” The sequel series followed the cast into high school and remained afloat for three seasons from 2008 to 2011.

“The Suite Life of Zack & Cody” brought Geoghan two Emmy nominations for Outstanding Children’s Program in 2007 and 2008. He previously worked as a sitcom writer on several shows including “Silver Spoons,” “The Facts of Life,” “Boys Will Be Boys,” “The Van Dyke Show” and more.

Popular on Variety

Geoghan also wrote for the stage. His play “Only Kidding” ran off Broadway for 500 performances, and “Light Sensitive” premiered at the Old Globe Theater in San Diego and has seen over 40 productions around the United States.

Geoghan started his career in comedy in 1973 by joining a popular New York comedy trio, Divided We Stand. Together, the trio became regulars at the Improvisation Cafe and other New York clubs like The Bitter End and Catch A Rising Star. They primarily spent their time touring colleges and other nightclubs across the country. He moved to Los Angeles with his wife Annie, also an actor, when he got the opportunity to start writing for television.

Outside of filmmaking, Geoghan enjoyed photography and crafts, like building model boats and planes. He was known for his joyous personality, kindness and humor. He is survived by his wife and his daughter.

title: Jim Geoghan Dies: ‘Suite Life Of Zack & Cody’ Co-Creator & Producer Was 79
summary: Jim Geoghan, who co-created and executive produced the Disney Channel’s touchstone sitcom The Suite Life of Zack & Cody, died Sunday, September 7, in Los Angeles. He was 79. His death was confirmed to Deadline by his daughter Genevieve Geoghan. A cause of death was not immediately available. Geoghan began his career in the early […]
content:
Jim Geoghan, who co-created and executive produced the Disney Channel’s touchstone sitcom The Suite Life of Zack & Cody, died Sunday, September 7, in Los Angeles. He was 79.

His death was confirmed to Deadline by his daughter Genevieve Geoghan. A cause of death was not immediately available.

Geoghan began his career in the early 1970s as part of a stand-up comedy trio called Divided We Stand, performing at such New York clubs as the Improvisation Cafe, The Bitter End, Catch A Rising Star and The Bottom Line. At colleges and nightclubs, the trio appeared on bills with Frankie Valli and the Four Seasons, The Beach Boys, The Commodores, Jimmy Buffet, The Righteous Brothers, Bill Withers, War, Sha Na Na and The Temptations.

Geoghan soon began writing for television on such series as Three’s Company, Sanford, Too Close For Comfort, The Facts of Life and The Van Dyke Show, among others. He wrote 18 episodes of Silver Spoons between 1983 and 1987, and around the same began writing and producing the form-bending It’s Garry Shandling’s Show; He was producer of that show from 1986 to 1990.

Other writing credits from the ’80s and ’90s include Kate & Allie, Mama’s Family, Amen and Family Matters, with producing credits on Silver Spoons and Family Matters, among others.

Dylan Sprouse, Cole Sprouse in ‘The Suite Life of Zack and Cody,’ co-created by Jim Geoghan Dean Hendler/Disney Channel/Everett Collection

In 2005, Geoghan co-created and co-executive produced (with Danny Kallis) The Suite Life of Zack and Cody for the Disney Channel, which ran for 87 episodes between 2005 and 2008, earning two Emmy nominations. The series starred Cole and Dylan Sprouse, Ashley Tisdale, Brenda Song and others as it followed the antics of a group of tween friends. A sequel series from 2008 to 2011, The Suite Life on Deck, featured the characters in high school.

After that show, Geoghan served as executive producer of The Suite Life of Karan & Kabir.

For the stage, Geoghan wrote Only Kidding, a play set in the world of stand-up comedy that opened Off Broadway at the American Jewish Theater in 1988 before transferring to the larger Westside Arts Theater. It ran for 500 performances and was nominated for two Drama Desk Awards, later being staged at regional theaters across the country.

In addition to his daughter, Geoghan is survived by Annie, his wife of 45 years.

title: ‘Saw: Genesis’ Creative Director Talks Multiplayer Build, Expanding The ‘Saw’ Mythology & Putting Players Through The Wringer
summary: During Gamescom 2026 in Germany, I got an extended preview of Saw: Genesis, the upcoming multiplayer horror game from Broken Mirror Games, Anshar Studios and Bloober Team. And while the game is set nearly a century before the events of the Saw films, the influence of the franchise’s most infamous figure is unmistakable even if […]
content:
During Gamescom 2026 in Germany, I got an extended preview of Saw: Genesis, the upcoming multiplayer horror game from Broken Mirror Games, Anshar Studios and Bloober Team. And while the game is set nearly a century before the events of the Saw films, the influence of the franchise’s most infamous figure is unmistakable even if John Kramer is nowhere to be found.

Set in the bleak aftermath of World War I, Saw: Genesis puts three players in the roles of the Accused, who must work together to survive a series of traps, puzzles and painful sacrifices. A fourth player takes on the role of the Judge, a potentially early predecessor to the philosophy that would eventually be associated with Kramer’s Jigsaw. The game turns Saw into a 3v1 asymmetrical multiplayer experience, but its developers were determined to preserve the twisted moral logic that has always been at the heart of the franchise. During my preview, I quickly learned that “survival” is a relative term — particularly when keeping an eye intact is part of the bargain.

I spoke with Anshar Studios’ creative director Damian Kocurek about bringing Saw into the multiplayer space, building out its mythology, and why, despite appearances, the Judges aren’t technically trying to kill you.

Watch on Deadline

DEADLINE: What did the talks with Lionsgate and James Wan look like when it came to approaching Saw: Genesis?

DAMIAN KOCUREK: Bloober Team has a previous connection with Lionsgate because they made 2019’s Blair Witch. So that’s why we [Anshar Studios] even started working on Saw. And during production, we did have calls with Lionsgate. They helped us a lot by making sure we didn’t break the IP and maintained a style that fit the narrative of that world. With James, we had a similar conversation, and he’s seen the game to make sure it works and that we are in constant contact.

Saw: Genesis Bloober Team

DEADLINE: This game takes place in the 1920s. Was there ever a conversation to have it in more modern times? Why did the 1920s feel right for you guys?

KOCUREK: We were looking for a few things at first. We wanted to have some creative freedom with it, create something original, and not conflict with the movies. There are 10 movies currently and more being made, so it’s very easy to create conflicts that take you out of that experience, so we wanted to build on top of it. Once we had that, we then looked for a setting, and the 1920s after the First World War—there is a lot to mine there. Many people are in trouble; there’s the great depression, and the country is trying to rebuild. So we thought, this is where a person could operate without being found out, so they could disappear into history and leave a very soft connection to something that happened later.

DEADLINE: How would you explain the narrative for this game for the folks at home?

KOCUREK: The basic setup for the game is that several characters are accused. Like the films, they are trapped and trying to escape. And in each match, there is one Judge, that’s the Jigsaw character. And the judge is “testing” those characters by trying to rehabilitate them. These characters have their own backgrounds that explain why they are judged and why they are in the test.

We will have two different Judges, and the one during this preview is called the Doctor. He’s a victim after taking part in the First World War, and he lost his jaw during that, so he’s trying to help people in the gruesome way of the Saw series.

Saw: Genesis Bloober Team

DEADLINE: Saw is known for its gnarly mutilation and traps, which I think you all certainly honor in this game. But what was something you couldn’t compromise on when approaching bringing this to life?

KOCUREK: There were a few things. So, even though we are making a multiplayer game, there’s a lot of lore-based stuff. What comes to mind mostly right now is that the Judges aren’t killers. They don’t try to kill those people.

DEADLINE: What? That is not what I experienced in my gameplay just moments ago. I had to gouge my eye out to live!

KOCUREK: The Judges are trying to help those people in their own twisted way [laughs]. That’s why I call this a rehabilitation. The Judges’ ultimate goal is to put the Accused in a Saw trap, and make them make a sacrifice, as you mentioned, but that’s the goal of the game. Not just killing people.

DEADLINE: No way.

KOCUREK: Well, yes, because in the movies, originally Jigsaw has that mantra about having that will to survive to be able to live. And for us it’s similar, but imperfect. Our Judges are more like, “You’ve committed sins, and you need to pay a pound of flesh, and only then can you move forward.” So, that’s the kind of similarities we wanted to keep.

DEADLINE: OK, but I still died several times.

KOCUREK: Yeah [laughs].

Saw: Genesis Bloober Team

DEADLINE: How did this game technology expand the world of the Saw movies?

KOCUREK: We were a little worried about what we could and couldn’t do. Because we’re in the first person, our game is more visceral because you don’t see things from the outside. The player has to be in it. So, a lot of the basics are more visceral because it happens to you as an avatar in the game, but it also limits us on what we can do because you don’t always see. A lot of the traps in Saw are very elaborate, and some devices target people’s backs or legs. So, we are trying to stay true to the movies as well, and we want people to have similar reactions to those things in the game.

And I think it works; we’ve seen people get very shocked by what they go through. I’m not sure it’s purely technological, but we definitely know games treat gore differently in many ways, especially given censorship levels. So, we are definitely different in that sense.

Saw: Genesis does not have a current scheduled release date as of this writing. However, they are in active playtest stages which you can sign up for here.

title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Trailer See A Fragile Peace Shattered As A New Threat Emerges
summary: Here’s an ominous phrase when one is speaking about Godzilla: “We didn’t finish the job like we thought.” That’s the opening line of the English-subtitled first trailer for Godzilla Minus Zero, Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel that is set two years after the events to his 2023 hit Godzilla Minus One. Equally troubling is this from logline […]
content:
Here’s an ominous phrase when one is speaking about Godzilla: “We didn’t finish the job like we thought.”

That’s the opening line of the English-subtitled first trailer for Godzilla Minus Zero, Takashi Yamazaki‘s sequel that is set two years after the events to his 2023 hit Godzilla Minus One. Equally troubling is this from logline for the new film: Just as humanity managed to cling to a hard-won peace, a new threat strikes, crushing hope in an instant. There is no third time. Everything ends here.

Watch the trailer above.

It’s 1949 Japan, and Ryunosuke Kamiki returns as Kōichi Shikishima, the ex-kamikaze pilot who originally was tasked with dealing with Godzilla in Minus One — and did so … right? “You saw it! Godzilla was blown to pieces,” he hear in the new trailer. Well, there was that little bit of the monster that was seen regenerating as it sunk into the ocean.

The returning cast also includes Minami Hamabe as Shikishima’s now-wife Noriko, along with Yuki Yamada, Hidetaka Yoshioka, Sakura Ando and Miou Tanaka. Masami Nagasawa joins the cast as Ms. Aoyama, a “forecasting prodigy” who suggests a Plan B.

Godzilla Minus One won the 2024 Oscar for its modestly budgeted visual effects and grossed $113.9 million worldwide with a near-even split from domestic and overseas. Yamazaki, who also did the effects for the new one, was the first director to win the VFX Academy Award since Stanley Kubrick for 2001: A Space Odyssey in 1969.

RELATED: ‘Godzilla Minus One’ Review: Toho’s Franchise Return Breathes Exciting New Life Into Japan’s Biggest Star

Godzilla Minus Zero is the first Japanese production to be filmed for Imax. It will have its world premiere September 26 at the New York Film Festival before screening in November as the centerpiece of the Tokyo Film Festival. The sequel attacks North American theaters on November 6.

title: Congress Begins Drafting 20% Federal Film Incentive With Trump’s Blessing (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Members of Congress are drafting legislation that would create a 20% federal film and TV incentive — with bonuses that could bring it as high as 30% — after President Trump endorsed the idea last week. The bill is expected to be introduced this month, and perhaps as soon as the end of next week, […]
content:
Members of Congress are drafting legislation that would create a 20% federal film and TV incentive — with bonuses that could bring it as high as 30% — after President Trump endorsed the idea last week.

The bill is expected to be introduced this month, and perhaps as soon as the end of next week, according to sources familiar with the process. Rep. Nathaniel Moran, a Republican from East Texas, is working on the bill with Rep. Linda Sanchez, a Democrat from Whittier, Calif. Both serve on the House Ways and Means Committee, which is responsible for tax legislation.

Rep. Laura Friedman, a Democrat from Burbank, Calif., has also been working with Rep. Brian Jack, a Republican from the Atlanta suburbs, on the bipartisan effort.

Popular on Variety

For the last year, the Motion Picture Association and entertainment unions have been advocating for an incentive that would compete with generous subsidies from the U.K., Canada, Australia and scores of other countries. Trump threw his weight behind the idea in a Truth Social post on Aug. 31, a development expected to unlock Republican support on Capitol Hill.

The draft legislation broadly aligns with the MPA’s request. The bill would offer a base credit of 20% of all labor costs, both below-the-line and above-the-line. A wide range of productions would be eligible, including reality TV and animation in addition to films and scripted TV shows, according to sources familiar with the legislation. It would not include news or sports broadcasts.

The bill would also include four “uplifts” meant to attract political support. According to a source, the bill would allow producers to claim an additional five percent if they meet one of these four criteria:

film in a rural opportunity zone

make an independent production

bring a certain amount of filming back to the U.S. from abroad

spend at least $10 million in 10 different states in a year

Producers could claim up to two of those uplifts, for a maximum of 30%. The federal tax credit would stack on top of state incentives, meaning that productions could see a total subsidy of 60% or more depending on where they film.

Supporters have argued that the incentive will not just help Los Angeles and New York — where the bulk of production takes place — but will also boost rural areas that currently have little filming and little or no state tax incentive.

The hope is that spreading production around will broaden support, much the way the state incentives in California and New York attracted votes from rural lawmakers by offering a bonus for filming outside of Los Angeles and New York City, respectively.

California lawmakers have also pushed for a bonus for any production in an area that was recently declared a federal disaster zone. (All of Los Angeles County would qualify due to the 2025 fires.) That is not included in the latest draft.

The tax credit could be used to offset federal income tax, or be sold to another taxpayer to offset their tax liability. It would not be refundable.

The bill has yet to go to the Joint Committee on Taxation, which will get a score on how much it would cost — though it is safe to say it will run into the billions of dollars. In his post last week, Trump argued that the cost would be “made up tenfold by the money pouring into the Treasury’s coffers.”

The MPA is expected to issue a report in the coming weeks that would expound on that claim, arguing that production creates a ripple effect that benefits the local economy.

Some supporters of the measure are optimistic about getting it through Congress as part of a tax bill during the lame duck session after the November election, though it may be more likely to happen next year.

“I would be very happy for it to happen in the lame duck,” Friedman said in an interview last week. “I can’t promise that’s possible. We’re going to try not only to get this done quickly, but to have all our ducks in a row.”

Friedman said that the discussions took on a new momentum after Trump got involved.

“I can’t tell you the number of texts that have come in from people who have offered to help,” she said.

She declined to discuss the specifics of the legislation, but said she is working to build a coalition across the country behind the idea.

“Everyone in every state loves movies and television,” she said. “Everyone benefits by this product being made here.”

title: Bruce Davis, Longtime AMPAS Executive Director, Dies at 83
summary: Bruce Davis, who served as Executive Director of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and helped develop the Margaret Herrick Library and Academy Film Archive, died Sept. 5 in Los Angeles. He was 83. Davis came to the Academy after chairing the theater department at Juniata College in Pennsylvania. He started out at […]
content:
Bruce Davis, who served as Executive Director of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and helped develop the Margaret Herrick Library and Academy Film Archive, died Sept. 5 in Los Angeles. He was 83.

Davis came to the Academy after chairing the theater department at Juniata College in Pennsylvania. He started out at the Academy overseeing public programming, and was named Executive Director in 1989. He retired from the Academy in 2011.

His tenure included two major achievements in film preservation: Davis worked with the city of Beverly Hills and Academy president Robert Wise to acquire rights to the 1928 building that became the Margaret Herrick Library, and oversaw the acquisition of the 1948 television studio in Hollywood that became the Academy Film Archive.

Popular on Variety

After retiring, Davis published the book “The Academy and the Award” about the origins and history of the Oscars.

He was known at the Academy for his wit, his writing skills and his Friday Lunch tradition where staff members from various departments would join him to eat and converse.

Born in Washington D.C., he became a film buff at a young age. At Juniata College, he founded the film department and led the theater department, as well as studying filmmaking at Columbia University.

He is survived by his wife Joann and four daughters: Brangien Davis (Daniel Spils); Alexandra Davis; Archer Davis (Tom Brown) and Roxanne Davis.

Donations may be made to Juniata College.

title: British TV Sector Revenues Hit $5.1 Billion Last Year Driven by U.S. Streamers: It ‘Underlines the Strength of the U.K. Production Market’
summary: British TV sector revenues hit £3.81 billion ($5.1 billion) last year, largely driven by U.S. streamers. The results were published by Pact, the U.K. producers trade group, who noted the figure represented a £149 million (4.1%) increase on 2024 revenues. They say it is driven primarily by streaming investment into the U.K. International TV revenue […]
content:
British TV sector revenues hit £3.81 billion ($5.1 billion) last year, largely driven by U.S. streamers.

The results were published by Pact, the U.K. producers trade group, who noted the figure represented a £149 million (4.1%) increase on 2024 revenues. They say it is driven primarily by streaming investment into the U.K.

International TV revenue accounted for 41.1% of total revenue in 2025, a figure of £1.57 billion, an increase of £214 million (15.8%) year-on-year. It is the first time the figure has grown since the post-Covid rebound 2022.

Pact noted that SVOD platforms such as Netflix, makers of “The Gentlemen” and “Black Doves,” and Amazon’s Prime Video, who boast “Clarkson’s Farm” and “L.O.L. Last One Laughing U.K.,” have continued to grow their commissioning budgets, resulting in all-time high investment into the country.

Popular on Variety

Conversely, however, revenues from domestic TV have fallen below £2 billion for the first time in five years (a 4.7% drop year on year) driven by a drop in U.K. commissions. Pact put this down to a small decline in spend from public service broadcasters such as the BBC and ITV and a “larger decline” in multichannel spend.

While international commissions accounted for 35% of all primary commissions, U.K. PSB network commissions decreased dropped from by 10% to 58%.

However £1.42 billion – at 85.9% the majority of revenue — still comes via PSB commissions.

According to Pact’s data producers are becoming increasingly canny about diversifying, with non-TV revenue growing by £34 million last year thanks to U.K. feature films, management and event production and advertising, among other revenue streams. Secondary rights revenue also grew by 12.7% to a record £575 million.

“Pact’s 2026 census underlines once again the strength of the U.K. production market in attracting inward investment, but also its vulnerability to declining domestic spend,” said Pact CEO, Nigel Warner.

“While it is welcome to see the proportion of investment in the nations and regions holding up, it is concerning that the pressures on new and smaller indies remain acute. A new settlement for a strong and sustainable BBC is urgently needed. The entrepreneurial spirit continues to drive the U.K.’s independent sector’s success, but we need to see growth in domestic PSB investment to help all parts of the production sector to thrive.”

title: Fired ‘60 Minutes’ Managing Editor Says New CBS Bosses Wanted ‘White House Talking Points in Our Reporting’ and ‘We Questioned Authority’
summary: Former “60 Minutes” managing editor Guy Campanile, who was fired in May alongside some top correspondents, has spoken out about his sudden ouster from the venerable CBS News program. In a private Facebook post obtained by The Guardian and recirculated by reporter Justin Baragona, Campanile wrote that “after some time and deep reflection,” he is […]
content:
Former “60 Minutes” managing editor Guy Campanile, who was fired in May alongside some top correspondents, has spoken out about his sudden ouster from the venerable CBS News program.

In a private Facebook post obtained by The Guardian and recirculated by reporter Justin Baragona, Campanile wrote that “after some time and deep reflection,” he is “now comfortable and prepared to talk about” his exit. Campanile, who worked at CBS News for 34 years, said he and his former colleagues — including fired correspondents Scott Pelley and Sharyn Alfonsi, to name a couple — “refused to be accomplices in the destruction of the most prestigious news program on American television.”

“We would not compromise our principles or reputations by jamming unverifiable notions or White House talking points into our reporting,” Campanile continued. “We objected when told to conduct interviews arranged by the administration. We insisted on asking the most challenging questions to business and political leaders without fear or favor. We did what reporters worth their salt do — we questioned authority … including our own bosses. That’s how the best newsrooms work. To be clear — we were told to leave because we insisted on doing our jobs.”

Popular on Variety

CBS did not immediately respond to Variety‘s request for comment.

The long-running newsmagazine has faced scandals, internal dissent and media backlash ever since CBS News was taken over by Paramount Skydance and the Ellison family, which installed Free Press founder Bari Weiss as editorial chief. Many former “60 Minutes” staffers have spoken out against the new regime, with Pelley alleging editorial decisions were made to “curry favor with the Trump administration” and “good people were silenced because they stood up for our audience” and “fairness against the forces of political bias.”

In his lengthy Facebook post, Campanile echoed many of Pelley’s concerns. “What has happened recently at ’60 Minutes’ – where I believe editorial independence has become a casualty of corporate priorities and ideological intrusion – was tragic,” he wrote. “But it was part of an inevitable progression in the cascade of afflictions that have devalued our most trusted sources of news.”

He issued the statement the same day “60 Minutes” teased its new season (premiering on Sept. 13) with a photo of its lineup of correspondents, including mainstays Lesley Stahl and Bill Whitaker alongside newcomers Norah O’Donnell and Ross Douthat.

Without naming names, Campanile criticized the ways in which information has become “commoditized in the attention economy.” “Making matters worse is the cadre of self-described influencers and on-line opinionists who market themselves as ‘journalists,'” he wrote. “Some have been given control of our most precious reporting institutions — including CBS News.”

Campanile concluded his remarks by saying he left CBS News “with my head held high and integrity intact.”

“I am excited about the opportunities ahead. In the meantime, I cannot remain silent as trust built over decades by my colleagues and mentors is wrecked,” he wrote. “The audience deserves so much better. Thomas Jefferson wrote, ‘Our liberty depends on the freedom of the press, and that cannot be limited without being lost.’ It’s dangerous to ignore his warning. As for my friends that remain at my former employer: Hold the line. Don’t give an inch because they will keep scraping away until there’s nothing left worth a damn.”

While Campanile did not mention specific incidents at “60 Minutes,” Pelley previously said “new management has instructed me to inject falsehoods and bias into a politically sensitive story” and that “recently, politicians have been invited to choose correspondents for interviews.” Last year, a segment about the “horrific treatment” of detainees deported from the U.S. to a prison in El Salvador was yanked by Weiss a few hours before airtime. Weiss said the segment “wasn’t ready,” while correspondents pushed back against their new boss, with Alfonsi claiming Weiss’ interference was “not an editorial decision, it is a political one.”

title: African American Film Critics Association Donates $25,000 to Black Film Hall of Fame – Film News in Brief
summary: The African American Film Critics Association (AAFCA) is donating $25,000 to the Black Film Hall of Fame.  “Supporting the Black Film Hall of Fame with this modest gift fits perfectly with ourorganization’s goals to align with institutions that serve to preserve Black storytelling content,” AAFCA President Gil Robertson IV said in a statement. Founded in […]
content:
The African American Film Critics Association (AAFCA) is donating $25,000 to the Black Film Hall of Fame.

“Supporting the Black Film Hall of Fame with this modest gift fits perfectly with ourorganization’s goals to align with institutions that serve to preserve Black storytelling content,” AAFCA President Gil Robertson IV said in a statement.

Founded in 2003, the Kansas City, Missouri-based museum and multicultural cultural center aims to preserve and celebrate Black cinema. The AAFCA is the largest collective of Black film critics in the world, and presents annual awards celebrations and special events that honor outstanding achievements in the entertainment industry.

“The Black Movie Hall of Fame is beyond thrilled by the generosity of Gil Robertson and AFFCA,” executive director and film critic Shawn Edwards said in a statement. “It’s a natural partnership as AAFCA and its roster of film critics represent one of the least talked about but most important aspects when acknowledging the history of Black cinema. For decades, Black film critics championed Black movies at a time when they were largely overlooked by the mainstream press. We look forward to building a lasting relationship with AAFCA and its membership.”

Popular on Variety

‘Donnie Darko’ Returns to Theaters for 25th Anniversary

Fathom Entertainment and Saga Arts are bringing “Donnie Darko” back to theaters in new 4K restoration on Oct. 2-4.

Beginning on “Donnie Darko Day,” the date in 1988 when the strange events of the film begin, the cult classic returns in its widest theatrical release for its 25th anniversary.

Originally released in 2001, “Donnie Darko” stars Jake Gyllenhaal as the titular troubled teen who receives a mysterious warning of the impending end of the world. The star-studded supporting cast features Jena Malone, Drew Barrymore, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Mary McDonnell, Holmes Osborne, Noah Wyle, Patrick Swayze and Seth Rogen.

The anniversary theatrical release also includes an exclusive introduction from writer and director Richard Kelly exploring the film’s legacy. The film was a box-office flop when it first premiered, but later found cult success in home video sales and reissues.

Watch the special 25th anniversary trailer below.

In film, Ruffalo has most recently been seen starring in Nimrods, the coming-of-age road trip comedy involving rock band Green Day, which released in August after premiering at last year’s Toronto Film Festival. Also seen in Marvel Studios’ Thor: Ragnarok, Ruffalo continues to be represented by Strand Entertainment, Bailey Brand Management, and Independent PR.

title: International Revenues Of $2.1B Boost British TV Makers, Census Finds, As Pact Warns BBC Must Avoid “Managed Decline”
summary: Revenue from Britain’s independent producers hit its second-highest total last year, despite spend from UK broadcasters falling beneath £2B ($2.7B) for the first time since 2020. The numbers from Pact come as the UK producers body warned that the BBC must avoid a situation of financial “managed decline.” The Pact Census shows UK television revenues […]
content:
Revenue from Britain’s independent producers hit its second-highest total last year, despite spend from UK broadcasters falling beneath £2B ($2.7B) for the first time since 2020. The numbers from Pact come as the UK producers body warned that the BBC must avoid a situation of financial “managed decline.”

The Pact Census shows UK television revenues were announced £1.99B for 2025, down 4.7% from £2.09B the previous year, but significant growth in international TV revenues and non-TV revenue propelled the overall figure up 4.1% to £3.81B.

This is a number only surpassed in a Covid-fuelled 2022, when the figure was just under £4B, with shows such as Netflix’s Adolescence among the biggest hits of 2025 and others such as Agatha Christie’s Seven Dials making noise this year.

The numbers reveal the increasing reliance on global streamer commissions, with traditional public service broadcasters under major financial stress and facing stark choices about their output.

Watch on Deadline

Pact, which represents a majority of the UK’s independent TV producers, revealed international revenue was £1.57B, up 15.8% on the £1.35B from the previous year and only behind 2022’s £1.62B. The number accounted for 41.1% of total revenues.

Warner, who was presenting the stats for the first time since replacing the long-serving John McVay, put this down to investment from the international streamers. He warned that commissions from the traditional domestic networks had fallen for the third consecutive year, placing significant pressure on small- and mid-sized production companies.

The slowdown was caused by multiple factors including “a contraction in the advertising market, a shift in viewers away from broadcast TV and continued inflationary pressures on productions costs.”

Warner also noted that subscription streamers now made 72.3% of all primary commissions from outside the UK, accounting for £916M, a figure that had risen from 27% over the past decade.

The stat highlighted how global streamers such as Netflix, Prime Video and Disney+ have become the top shoppers by this metric. In the early-to-mid 2010s, most commissions came from the U.S. cable giants, who would order shows for channels across their international footprints.

Meanwhile, UK production companies were also benefitting from post-Hollywood strike recovery and from international finished tape sales returning to “usual levels” after a sharp 26.8% decline in 2024 brought about by production backlogs easing.

Non-TV revenue (which includes online publishing, talent management, promotions, PR and feature films) was £258M, well up on last year’s £224M and above the previous record, £236M, which was posted back in 2013.

Furthermore, the secondary rights market increased by £65M to reach £575M, as the reality of a market where producers must be more entrepreneurial was laid bare.

“[The growth is] a testament to the demand and to UK content, but it could also suggest that producers might be increasingly relying on future rights revenue to help finance production,” said Warner.

During a presentation to press, it was put to Warner that producers are facing a major the threat to the Terms of Trade have underpinned their businesses and allowed them to retain rights to shows commissioned by British networks since 2003.

Channel 4, often considered the closest friend to the indie sector for its publisher-broadcaster model, is still working on plans to launch an in-house division, while Sky is buying ITV and BBC Director General Matt Brittin has cquestioned whether Terms of Trade rules are fit for purpose in the modern era.

“The fundamentals of [the Terms of Trade] remain critically important to the health of the independent sector and have underpinned the growth of the independent sector over the past 25 years,” said Warner, adding Pact was in continual discussions with each broadcaster and pointing to a new deal closed with Paramount’s 5 in March.

Warner said the amount of third-party funding going into budgets was among the most “significant changes we’ve seen in recent years” and added that “now we’re seeing broadcasters contributing considerably less in terms of the initial financial cost of production.”

The picture will become clearer once Channel 4’s in-house unit is established, an arrangement with a merged Sky and ITV was in place and talks with the BBC over terms were concluded, added Warner.

“In an environment where indies are contributing ever more towards the cost of production in the first place, they need to be in the position to recoup that investment themselves, and the rights become even more important,” he said.

BBC under pressure

The Pact Census numbers will make for unwelcome reading for Britain’s public service broadcasters, and in particular the BBC, which is looking to make up to £500M in costs savings amid a funding crisis.

Pact once again suggested the BBC should look to replace the current licence fee funding model, which is under strain with an increasing number of viewers refusing to pay, with an alternative such as a household levy similar to Germany. “There’s a strong logic in moving in that direction,” said Warner in response to a Deadline question, adding it would remove the opportunity to evade paying.

“At the moment, I don’t see much of an alternative being presented other than simply carrying on the way we are, which risks the continuation of a decline in income and expenditure investment.”

Pact policy director Emily Oyama added this would mean “less money to spend and therefore less money being spent,” adding this represents “managed decline.”

This year was the first in a quarter of a century in which McVay was not CEO of the producers organization. Warner replaced him in March this year.

title: Paramount Warns CA AG Bonta & WGA Of WBD Merger Fallout & “Financial Consequences If Their Challenge Ultimately Fails”
summary: Just weeks before Paramount Skydance starts being on the hook for the vaunted $7-million-a-day ticking fee to Warner Bros Discovery shareholders, the David Ellison-run company today pushed hard once again for the Writers Guild of America, California and 11 other states to pony up a nearly $2 billion bond in the antitrust battle over the […]
content:
Just weeks before Paramount Skydance starts being on the hook for the vaunted $7-million-a-day ticking fee to Warner Bros Discovery shareholders, the David Ellison-run company today pushed hard once again for the Writers Guild of America, California and 11 other states to pony up a nearly $2 billion bond in the antitrust battle over the $111 billion ParaBros merger.

In fact, with an implication they might just close the currently paused deal anyway if a federal judge doesn’t see things their way, Paramount pushed very hard today.

“Ticking fees like the one Paramount faces are extraordinarily rare, in part because they are extraordinarily expensive,” the multi-law firm repped Paramount said Tuesday in a tense reply brief over the contested big bucks bond and the long wait until the March 2027 trial. “It would be incredibly risky to add such fees solely to deter private litigation; if the merging parties ultimately lose the antitrust litigation, the payor of the ticking fee would be left with an enormous bill and no merger,” the still Melrose lot HQ’d company added.

Watch on Deadline

“And there is no contention that this is such a case, Paramount’s lawyers went on to say. “Here, Paramount added the ticking fee in a highly competitive bidding war with Netflix, confident that its transaction is legal under established U.S. and foreign antitrust laws and would clear the relevant regulatory hurdles well before those fees started accruing,” they noted of the roller coaster ride to snag WBD from the streamer and the ultimate deal that was given the thumbs up by “good friend” Donald Trump‘s Department of Justice earlier this summer.

RELATED: Here Are Five Things In The Media Mix As 2026 NFL Season Kicks Off, Including Billion-Dollar Rights Fight

Insisting on the importance of over 60 other jurisdictions that have approved the merger (though the vast majorities of those approvals were limited to the immediate territory of the specific nations), Paramount don’t quite come out and call the states, the scribes and their long threatened July 13 lawsuit out as dirty dealers — but they get damn close.

“Paramount provided unrebutted evidence that, but for the Order, it may suffer $1.88 billion in damages,” the 22-page filing says with telling mentions of the halted Nexstar/Tegna merger throughout. “Critically, the states never dispute that evidence or otherwise contest that Paramount will suffer financial injury as a result of the Order, both from the ticking fee and the incremental financing costs—a financial harm that the states outright ignore. Nor do they deny that Paramount would close this transaction by September 30, 2026, but-for the stipulated injunction. For purposes of this motion, then, the states have conceded that Paramount provided evidence to establish $1.88 billion in potential damages.”

RELATED: Tom Cruise Backs Paramount’s 30-Movies-A-Year Promise In WBD Merger: “I Think It’s Awesome”

Take a deep breath and take a look at that September 30 mention, that could be the vanishing point here, if you know what I mean? Also, recall that Paramount and Warner Bros agreed two weeks after the AGs and WGA hit them in court not to seal the merger deal until June 1, 2027 or when the legal challenges end — whatever comes first.

Shifting focus again, the filing states full stop: “Because Paramount has established $1.88 billion in damages it will potentially suffer as a direct result of being wrongfully enjoined, the Court should grant the motion.”

David Ellison Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

Lamenting Ellison’s “old stale promise” of putting out more movies, Bonta wants structural remedies in the ParaBros merger in order to back off. Whatever has been floated behind closed boardroom doors (which has not included peeling off CNN as of yet), it hasn’t gotten structural enough for the reelection seeking AG.

As of today, with no real settlement talks underway, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin has a September 24 hearing on the books to discuss the bond issue. Also on the non-court calendar is the October 1 date when the over $635 million a quarter ticking fees begins. FYI: That October 1 date is the same date that Paramount has supposedly given for settlement talks to begin or they may start looking at a corporate move out of blue state California to a red state.

Now facing a move from Iowa and Montana to take the whole dispute to the Supreme Court, Bonta and crew have already called the Paramount relocation whispers “blackmail.” A much hyped settlement sit-down was scuttled at the 11th hour by the Meta and Nexstar/Tegna fighting Golden State AG amidst accusations that Paramount was leaking details of confidential discussions. An allegation that Paramount denies.

Getty Images

Battle lines and alliances are clearly drawn with everyone from Tom Cruise, to CA’s current and next Governor, the Christopher Nolan-run DGA, IATSE, Ari Emanuel and everyone in between offering encouragement for a putting down of swords and a settlement. On the other hand, as big names link arms with Block the Merger activists, another report submitted to the L.A. Board of Supervisors warns of possible big job losses for the region if the deal goes through. The Department of Economic Opportunity adds to the gloom and doom by predicting that the mega-merger could cost L.A. County billions in wages and hundreds of millions in tax revenue.

With all that as the backdrop, Paramount said Tuesday in a separate statement that “if plaintiffs insist that this transaction is paused during the pendency of their lawsuit, they must accept the financial consequences if their challenge ultimately fails.” They added: “Paramount agreed to delay closing to facilitate a prompt resolution of the case, while expressly preserving its legal rights and we continue to honor that agreement. We are not asking the district court to lift the no-close order, but to require enforcement of the bond that protects our financial interests while the litigation remains pending.”

AG Bonta’s office response to today’s Paramount brief was brief unto itself. “We believe Paramount’s motion has no merit and look forward to presenting our case in court at the September 24th hearing” the state DOJ asserted

Having come up short weeks ago in its efforts to gain a faster trial in the challenge from the Rob Bonta-led coalition of state Attorneys Genera and the scribes’ union, Paramount moved on August 17 for its merger opponents to hand over some cash. Cash that is designed for the multi-billion dollar company and its loaded owner(s) to cover the “extraordinary losses” the long wait until a judgement is given on ParaBros Yes or ParaBros No.

“Now that trial is scheduled for March 2027, roughly four months after the trial date proposed by Defendants, and more than half a year from now, Paramount seeks the bond to which it is statutorily entitled,” the once Shari Redstone owned company wrote in its motion last month

Needless to say AG Bonta, New York AG Letitia James, the WGA and the rest of the roadblockers took a very different stance.

“Whatever regret Paramount may feel for its commitments to Warner Bros., to Plaintiff States, to the WGA,1 and to the Court, it cannot show that the Court acted ‘improvidently’ in signing the joint stipulation,” the WGA and the 12 AGs responded on September 1. “Nor can Paramount show why the public or a non-profit labor union should underwrite its acquisition of Warner Bros.”

“In the alternative, if the Court grants Paramount’s motion, it should impose a nominal bond of $10,000.”

That would be a joke, if anyone was still laughing in this bitter stand-off.

title: Casey Affleck’s ‘Company’ Earns 4.5-Minute Ovation At Venice World Premiere
summary: Casey Affleck returned to the Venice Film Festival on Tuesday with his latest directorial effort, Company, which earned a 4½-minute ovation following its debut screening inside the Sala Grande.  There was an enthusiastic response, but Affleck and the cast left as applause was ongoing, and it died off. Star Nick Nolte got an extra-rousing cheer […]
content:
Casey Affleck returned to the Venice Film Festival on Tuesday with his latest directorial effort, Company, which earned a 4½-minute ovation following its debut screening inside the Sala Grande.

There was an enthusiastic response, but Affleck and the cast left as applause was ongoing, and it died off.

Star Nick Nolte got an extra-rousing cheer when he was presented at the beginning of the screening. Ben Affleck was there to support his brother. sitting beside the cast and clapping enthusiastically and filming audience below.

Directed by Affleck from a screenplay he wrote with Ron Hansen, Company opens on a winter night in 1975. A mysterious woman named Evelyn arrives uninvited at a holiday gathering and tells the story of Tom, an aging hermit who rescued a stranded actress during a Colorado blizzard in 1953. To pass the night, the actress recounts an older tale of a farming couple who take in a troubled young drifter as a series of grisly murders spreads fear across the frontier.

Watch on Deadline

RELATED: Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews

The official synopsis reads: “As the stories intertwine across generations, Company becomes a meditation on grief, vengeance, forgiveness and the quiet acts of compassion that can heal even the deepest wounds.”

Discussing the film’s premise at Tuesday’s official press conference, Affleck said the feature wasn’t an “explicitly political movie,” but he also isn’t “impervious to the world around me.”

“I was responding in part to all the raging conflicts in the world, and to things inside myself,” he said of the film’s origins.

Company stars Nick Nolte, Ben Mendelsohn, Adelaide Clemens, Scoot McNairy, Emily Alyn Lind, Caylee Cowan, Atticus Affleck and Indiana Affleck. Casey Affleck was last in Venice as an actor with Bill Pohlad’s Dreamin’ Wild in 2022. His previous effort as a director was Light of My Life (2019), which debuted at the Berlin Film Festival.

RELATED: 48 Of The Most Anticipated Movies Of 2026

Producers on the project include Steven Schneider and Roy Lee via Spooky Features, Catherine Caylee Cowan, Dan Lawler, Affleck, Sean Patrick O’Reilly, K. Asher Levin, Enzo Marc, and Anthony Katagas.

The executive producers include Ben Ross via Image Nation Studios, Rami Yasin for Spooky Pictures, Ronnie Exley and Jeremy Ross via Rabbits Black, Ron McLeod, Dr. Terence Chan, Brian Meng, and Maria Breese for 3:33 Creative Productions, and Jonathan Miller.

Melanie Goodfellow contributed to this report.
