title: Chernin Entertainment Expands Film Team With Key Hire, Promotions (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Chernin Entertainment, the prolific independent film and TV producer founded by former News Corp. chairman Peter Chernin, has expanded its in-house film team. Under movies chief David Ready, the film unit has had big wins this year in theaters (“Backrooms”) and on streaming (Netflix’s “The Last House”), and will continue to scale its slate. To […]
content:
Chernin Entertainment, the prolific independent film and TV producer founded by former News Corp. chairman Peter Chernin, has expanded its in-house film team.

Under movies chief David Ready, the film unit has had big wins this year in theaters (“Backrooms”) and on streaming (Netflix’s “The Last House”), and will continue to scale its slate.

To fulfill that effort is new hire Marisa Paiva, who joins as an executive vice president of film. Paiva got her start Fox 2000 and spent over 13 years at the studio, working on literary adaptations like “Water for Elephants” and “Life of Pi.” She later oversaw the award-winning “Hidden Figures” and “The Woman in the Window.” She joined 3000 Pictures in 2019, developing “Lady Chatterley’s Lover” for Netflix and spearheading high-profile acquisitions like “Broken Country,” which Paiva will executive produce with Hello Sunshine.

Paiva will join fellow EVP Brady Fujikawa, who joined the studio last year from Lionsgate. Fujikawa rises from his previous title of development and production lead. He oversaw the hot package “High Side,” which will put Timothée Chalamet in a motocross seat for director James Mangold. Fujikawa is also shepherding “Palm Grove,” starring Kate Hudson and Ana de Armas and directed by Kornél Mundruczó; and “One Month Mark,” a Jennifer Lawrence rom-com set up at Apple. He was previously at Good Universe (“Blockers,” “Good Boys”), and helped expand the John Wick universe at Lionsgate.

Popular on Variety

Meanwhile, Samantha Nisenboim has been named senior vice president of film. Her producer credits include “The Lego Batman Movie,” The Tomorrow War” and “Renfield.” She is currently producing two feature films at Chernin, including the Netflix thriller “The Big Fix” starring Mark Wahlberg and Riz Ahmed.

Finally, Max Gains has been named creative executive. He began his career at Paramount before joining 21 Laps, where he spent six years working his way up from Shawn Levy’s assistant. His projects included “Deadpool & Wolverine,” “The Adam Project” and “Free Guy.”

Ready told Variety that the company has “built a strong foundation and a slate we really believe in, and now we have the team to build out our next chapter. Marisa, Brady, Samantha, and Max are the kind of executives you want on your team – smart, relentless, deeply connected and driven by great material.”

Chernin recently inked a new multi-year, first-look feature film deal with Apple Studios. In January, Mediawan announced an agreement to acquire Chernin parent The North Road Company. The combined entity will have major creative hubs across five continents and capabilities spanning all genres and formats.

title: Axios Co-Founders Urge Wielding AI to Help ‘Simplify’ Your Life in New Book
summary: The co-founders of Axios popularized the “Smart Brevity” mantra for years. Now, in the age of AI, comes another: “Simplify.” Such is the name of a new book by Mike Allen, Jim VandeHei and Roy Schwartz, who co-founded the political news site in 2016 to try and help get people smarter faster. “Simplify,” out Tuesday, […]
content:
The co-founders of Axios popularized the “Smart Brevity” mantra for years. Now, in the age of AI, comes another: “Simplify.”

Such is the name of a new book by Mike Allen, Jim VandeHei and Roy Schwartz, who co-founded the political news site in 2016 to try and help get people smarter faster. “Simplify,” out Tuesday, expands on that mission, serving as an instructive guide for readers to use AI to excise distractions and boost their personal and professional lives. It’s a mantra VandeHei says worked for the company, prompting the trio over the last two and a half years to figure out how to adapt it for a tome.

“I never sort of set out with, ‘Hey, I’m looking for opportunities to write a book,’” he says. “We really got inspired to write Simplify after just seeing the amazing effect it was having on our company, and also applying some of the stuff personally and seeing the effect it was having on me personally. In some ways you become almost childlike, like I want to share this with other people because it’s making such a such a huge difference.”

Popular on Variety

The book features a mixture of anecdotes from their personal lives that detail how the three “confront” their challenges, “delete” such distractions to “amplify” their own lives. VandeHei, for example, carves out a dedicated hour for the gym every day and says no to most social functions he doesn’t deem strictly necessary, as does Allen. The latter also had to unlearn his lengthy writing habits from his days spearheading Politico’s “Playbook” newsletter for Axios’ “AM” newsletter. Schwartz, who now runs Axios’ business-focused venture Axios HQ, flipped the barrier his dyslexia provided into a tool to break down complicated topics into simple points, while MS NOW star Rachel Maddow explains her logic behind her all-black uniform for her eponymous primetime show. (“I no longer wanted to spare even the infinitesimal effort of choosing a daily variation on my standard, boring outfit,” she says in the book.)

“We came to all this the hard way, and we came to it by making mistakes,” Allen says. “But the payoff for having this rigor and having this discipline is the third part of ‘amplify,’ and that’s where you cash the check for doing the hard work. That you are able to spend more time on what you’re uniquely good at, and what brings you joy.“

AI is as much a character in the book as any of the co-founders or the company itself, reflecting Axios’ ethos that the technology will be a “moonshot” for its growth (a sentiment that came days after it laid off 11 staffers in March). The company’s enthusiastic adoption of the technology has also made its way into several columns written by VandeHei and Allen, along with a post written by publisher Nick Johnston that drew some mockery over his admission that he used AI as a guide while reading “The Last of the Mohicans.”

“I don’t have a lot of friends that are reading the classics at the beach,” Allen says in his defense, urging people to read the piece. “Nick is an actual book reader, and he’s someone who’s reading James Fenimore Cooper, reading ‘The Last of the Mohicans,’ reading, on paper, in hardcover, a classic, and he’s using AI as a smart friend to talk about it as he went along.”

The co-founders warn in the book about the risk of “slop,” both human and AI-generated, interfering with the goals people set out for themselves and creating a trickle-down effect for others, leading to unnecessary work. Instead, they suggest deploying AI agents to help with everything from clearing calendars to posing questions over whether a task, menial or otherwise, is necessary.

“There’s no hero in this story other than you,” VandeHei says. “You have to be the one who kind of really understands the technology, comes at it eyes wide open, figures out when it could be of great benefit to you. That you’re aware of the seductive nature of it, you’re aware of where you could start seeing the parts of your brain that matter most. Just like the burden in the information age on the internet was on the individual, the burden really remains on the individual.”

Schwartz applies this mindset to his business-side clients as well, fusing AI with both “Smart Brevity” and “Simplify” approaches to, say, break down research documents for a healthcare company into bullet points so they can get the information faster. The book also ends with a QR code to help readers use an AI agent to hold themselves accountable to the “Simplify” mantra.

“I hate the category of self-help, but we’ve all read those books, wanted to implement them, and had trouble implementing,” he says. “I think it’s natural, right, to not be able to hold yourself fully accountable. But AI doesn’t care.”

VandeHei understands that the “Simplify” mindset can’t be applied universally, especially when life throws unexpected challenges in one’s way. But clearing up as much as possible in one’s life frees up more bandwidth toward some of those other tasks, which he says is ultimately the book’s goal.

“There’s no doubt that there’s buckets of life that are inherently deep and inherently complex,” he says. “You want to be able to free up enough time so that you actually can deal with complexity when it’s required, or you can deal with depth when you need to deal with it, and so that’s why you have to simplify all the things that can be simplified. Not everything can. We’re not dumb. But the more that you can simplify — the fewer meetings, the less time wasted, the fewer projects that don’t need to be done — that gives you the time to more thoughtfully think about and take action on the things that require depth and complexity.”

title: ‘The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time’ 40th Anniversary Remake Sets Nintendo Switch 2 Release Date (Gaming News Roundup)
summary: Celebrating 40 years of gameplay, an updated version of “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” will be available for Nintendo Switch 2 on Nov. 5. The remake will have overhauled visuals, fully voiced cutscenes, expanded character dialogue, symphonic orchestral music, reworked camera and movement controls and more. In this game, the main playable protagonist, […]
content:
Celebrating 40 years of gameplay, an updated version of “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” will be available for Nintendo Switch 2 on Nov. 5.

The remake will have overhauled visuals, fully voiced cutscenes, expanded character dialogue, symphonic orchestral music, reworked camera and movement controls and more. In this game, the main playable protagonist, Link’s, milestone adventure has been reborn for a whole new era.

This version of “Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” will have improved performance and presentation, greater movement and control and a more immersive Hyrule. Players can now sing or hum one of Link’s learned ocarina melodies within range of the Nintendo Switch 2 system’s built-in microphone, and he’ll perform the song in the game.

Popular on Variety

For additional information about new features and enhancements coming to “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” or to preorder, please visit Nintendo Store or Nintendo eShop.

See more gaming news from the week below.

TRAILERS

“Spyro: A Realm Beyond” has released its first look at Arcadian Vale in honor of Spyro Community Day.

The game’s region is a calm, vibrant location consisting of natural beauty. Per the game’s description, “Across the scene are cascading waterfalls tumbling down from towering cliffs. Ancient stone structures and weathered monuments rise from the terrain while lush greenery blankets the valley floor, creating a destination that feels magical and alive.”

Also featuring friendly creatures, Arcadian Vale is designed to capture the whimsy of the “Spyro” universe.

See the first look below.

NEWLY ANNOUNCED GAMES

Nintendo unveiled “Metroid Ravenous” and “Kirby and the World Beyond” during a Nintendo Direct presentation Wednesday, noting both newly announced games will be available on the Nintendo Switch 2 next year.

Samus Aran is back with even more of a fight for survival in “Metroid Ravenous.” The game’s amiibo collection will feature Samus and Chozo Statue figures at its launch, while a third amiibo of Samus in her Metroid Suit will be bundled in a special edition that also includes a steel case for the game. Both releases will launch Jan. 28, and pre-orders are available now.

“Kirby and the World Beyond” is a 3D adventure for Kirby, where the character’s Copy Abilities allow players to freely explore Kirby’s universe. The game will debut in spring 2027, timed with the 35th anniversary for the Kirby series.

See first look photos below.

EVENTS

PAX West is returning to the Seattle Convention Center next Labor Day weekend from Sept. 3 to Sept. 6, following this year’s event.

The gaming event will also debut PAX Unplugged Houston, the new iteration of PAX expos that will take place June 25 to June 27 at the George R. Brown Convention Center in Houston, Texas. Badges will be available to purchase later this year.

On the East Coast, PAX Unplugged 2026 returns to the Pennsylvania Convention Center Dec. 6 to Dec. 8, while PAX East 2027 will be held in Boston at the Thomas M. Menino Convention & Exhibition Center April 22 to April 25.

LIVE EVENTS

Select AMC theaters will screen the live broadcast of Epic Games’ 2026 Rocket League World Championship Finals.

For the first time, fans will be able to watch Rocket League teams compete for the $1.2 million prize pool on Sept. 20 at 50 AMC locations nationwide, including Chicago, Boston, New York and Los Angeles. The event is estimated to run for approximately eight hours, and tickets are on sale now. Attendees will also receive a commemorative Rocket League ticket that allows players to redeem in-game cosmetics.

“Such a big part of the magic of movie theaters is their ability to bring people together for unforgettable shared experiences, and a live event like the Rocket League World Championship is a great example of that,” said Ellen Copaken, the senior vice president of business development at AMC Theatres. “We’re excited to give fans the opportunity to watch esports’ biggest stage unfold live on massive screens, surrounded by fellow Rocket League fans.”

title: Netflix Snaps Up Australian Doc Series ‘2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback’ Ahead Of TIFF Bow
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Netflix has picked up Australian documentary series 2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback globally ahead of its world premiere at Toronto.   The four-part Australian documentary series, produced by Blackfella Films for SBS and NITV is the only documentary among the ten series selected for TIFF’s Primetime program. The series examines the events and far-reaching […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Netflix has picked up Australian documentary series 2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback globally ahead of its world premiere at Toronto.

The four-part Australian documentary series, produced by Blackfella Films for SBS and NITV is the only documentary among the ten series selected for TIFF‘s Primetime program.

The series examines the events and far-reaching repercussions of the two fatal shots fired in 2.6 seconds that ended the life of 19-year-old Kumanjayi Walker, and prompted a national debate over justice, policing and race in Australia.

The series from director Darren Dale will premiere on Netflix in early 2027. Writer is Andrew Boe, with Dale also producing. Executive Producers are Andrew Boe and Jacob Hickey.

Watch on Deadline

Darren Dale, Blackfella Films Producer, said: “2.6 Seconds is a shocking story about the collision of race and power that is uniquely Australian but one I’ve always believed also has global resonance. Netflix coming on board ahead of our TIFF premiere is confirmation of that belief and I cannot wait to see how international audiences respond to this powerful series.”

Amanda Duthie, Content Director Netflix ANZ commented: “Some stories stay with you long after the screening, and 2.6 Seconds is one of those. Netflix is honoured to bring this deeply moving Australian documentary to Netflix audiences around the world, giving a powerful and important story the opportunity to resonate far beyond our shores.”

2.6 Seconds is a co-commission between SBS and NITV with the production of Blackfella Films in association with PAW Media. Major production investment came from Screen Australia’s First Nations Department in association with SBS. It was financed with support from Screen NSW and produced in association with All3Media International.

title: Mike Epps Set For ‘My Father’s Son’ Comedy Series In Development At Netflix
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Mike Epps, one of Netflix’s most popular stand-ups and star of its sitcom The Upshaws, is expanding his relationship with the streamer via My Father’s Son, a new comedy series he’ll star in and exec produce, sources tell Deadline. Reps for Netflix declined to comment. We’re told this is a father-son story, inspired by the life of […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Mike Epps, one of Netflix‘s most popular stand-ups and star of its sitcom The Upshaws, is expanding his relationship with the streamer via My Father’s Son, a new comedy series he’ll star in and exec produce, sources tell Deadline.

Reps for Netflix declined to comment. We’re told this is a father-son story, inspired by the life of Chris “Comedian CP” Powell, the rising stand-up from Detroit. Plot details are being kept under wraps.

Epps exec produces alongside his producing partner Niles Kirchner, Bob Teitel at State Street, and Maurice Williams (Entergalactic), who will also serve as writer-showrunner. Doug Banker is also aboard to exec produce via Five All in the Fifth, as are Trevor Engelson of Underground and Comedian CP.

The history surrounding this project is interesting as it’s now going through its third round of development. Initially, it was set up as a live-action show for HBO Max, before moving to Netflix for development as an animated series. The current iteration is for live-action.

Watch on Deadline

Currently on his We Them Ones tour, Epps is coming off the release of his latest Netflix special, Delusional, which premiered globally on January 27, delivering his strongest launch to date on the platform with nearly four million views in its first week. This was Epps’ fifth special for the platform, which earlier this year inked a deal for two more from him, as we reported exclusively.

When it comes to Netflix’s creative partnership with Epps, which goes back more than a decade, the numbers tell the story. Since 2023, when Netflix began releasing its What We Watched reports, his specials have racked up 20.4M views. A veteran comic who’s been working since the mid-’90s, he exec produced and starred in The Upshaws, a multi-cam about a working-class family set in his Indiana hometown, which was nominated for 10 NAACP Image Awards, with Epps winning for Outstanding Actor in a Comedy Series in 2024.

Epps has also been seen on shows like I’m a Virgo, Survivor’s Remorse and Winning Time, with film credits including The Underdoggs, You People and Dolemite Is My Name, to name just a few. Most recently, he’s been seen in Netflix’s Kevin Hart comedy 72 Hours, as well as Paramount+’s The Varnell Hill Show. He is repped by Kirchner, IAG and Yorn, Levine, Barnes.

Comedian CP is coming off the special Sunday After Six, which made its way to BET after premiering on Veeps. He both co-produced and appeared in the shows Diarra from Detroit and How to Die Alone, with additional acting credits including Fox’s Empire, Comedy Central’s Detroiters and HBO Max’s Love Life. Upcoming, he’ll be seen in the Barbershop TV series from Prime Video. He is repped by Innovative Artists, Artists First and Yorn, Levine, Barnes.

Williams is repped by WME, Mosaic and Lichter, Grossman, Nichols.

title: Aaron Dominguez Signs With Paradigm; Joins Cast Of ‘Power: Origins’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Aaron Dominguez has signed with Paradigm for representation. Additionally, Dominguez has joined the cast of the upcoming “Power” franchise spinoff sequel, Starz’s Power: Origins, which follows the events of the Power Book III: Raising Kanan series finale. Details regarding his character are under wraps. From Sascha Penn, Power: Origins will expand the “Power” Universe by delving into […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Aaron Dominguez has signed with Paradigm for representation.

Additionally, Dominguez has joined the cast of the upcoming “Power” franchise spinoff sequel, Starz‘s Power: Origins, which follows the events of the Power Book III: Raising Kanan series finale. Details regarding his character are under wraps.

From Sascha Penn, Power: Origins will expand the “Power” Universe by delving into the origin story of fan-favorite characters Ghost (Spence Moore II), Tommy (Charlie Mann), and Kanan (Mekai Curtis). The three are ambitious young entrepreneurs on the rise, determined to make their mark on the streets of New York City.

Starz calls Origins “a fun, rambunctious exploration of a new time period in the Power franchise that will highlight the unbridled audacity of young men on the rise, determined to become legends in the game.”

Watch on Deadline

Dominguez is perhaps best known for starring opposite Selena Gomez, Steve Martin, and Martin Short in the critically acclaimed Hulu series Only Murders in the Building. He played the fan-favorite character Oscar Torres, better known as Tie-Dye Guy, in the show’s first season. Next, he pivoted to film with a role in A24’s The Inspection from writer and director Elegance Bratton, followed by the Amazon Studios rom-com Sitting in Bars With Cake, starring opposite Bette Midler and Odessa A’zion.

Dominguez’s small screen credits also include the new Gossip Girl, from Joshua Safran for HBO Max, and Netflix’s first medical series Pulse, from Carlton Cuse. Additional film credits include the Shaft sequel for Warner Bros., and starring alongside Madison Iseman in the feature Witchboard. Most recently, he was seen working alongside Xotchil Gomez in the horror feature Hive from director Felipe Vargas.

Dominguez continues to be repped by Alexander White Agency, Canopy Media Partners, and Imprint PR.

title: Trump & Other Major Hurdles Ahead For Federal Film & TV Tax Incentive Bill Becoming Reality
summary: Among many D.C. lobbyists, when the bet is on whether a piece of legislation will pass Congress or not, the rule of thumb always is to take the latter. Yet, a long-desired federal film and television tax incentive that’s suddenly coming to life with the recent backing of Donald Trump could prove the exception. Maybe. […]
content:
Among many D.C. lobbyists, when the bet is on whether a piece of legislation will pass Congress or not, the rule of thumb always is to take the latter. Yet, a long-desired federal film and television tax incentive that’s suddenly coming to life with the recent backing of Donald Trump could prove the exception. Maybe.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are drafting legislation, with current plans for a 20% incentive and an additional 5% to 10% for rural areas or spread across several states. A bill could be introduced this month, with some announcement on the status expected when Congress returns next week, and the details are not set in stone.

“This is the best opportunity now we’ve had to get this done in really decades,” Sen. Adam Schiff (D-CA) said on CNN this week. On Tuesday, Schiff complimented talks among the White House, House members and some of his fellow Senators, but cautioned a deal is not yet done. “Negotiations are ongoing,” Schiff, who Trump has long attacked personally and politically, told Deadline.

Watch on Deadline

So far, the anticipated multibillion-dollar federal incentive also has the advantage of backing by some members of the House Ways & Means Committee, which controls the purse strings, and that support is bipartisan. Among those said to be working on legislation are two members — Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-TX) and Rep. Linda Sanchez (D-CA) — each from a state that has a lot of production in its past, present and hopefully future.

RELATED: Sacramento’s Mad Legislative Dash To Fix Tax Credits SNAFU, Get Post-Production Incentive Passed, Or Not

That said, even though proponents see the best prospects in years for passage of something, there still is a long way to go despite the backing of a fickle POTUS and the other good intentions.

Here are some of the hurdles ahead:

Timing

With so few days left in the legislative session before the midterms, there just isn’t time left to pass legislation before then, especially a bill that is still in the works. Advocates including studio representatives and union officials are expected to up their PR campaign in the coming weeks, particularly if there is a concrete proposal on the table.

RELATED: The Enemy Of My Enemy: Left And Right Search For Common Ground To Prop Up U.S. Entertainment Business

That leaves the question of when. The lame-duck session will likely focus on whether an agreement can be reached on an overall bill to fund the government, with an expiration of December 11. If the past is any guide, it’s much more likely that the bill would be attached to some end-of-year funding measure than as stand-alone legislation.

Midterm results

While a number of Republicans and Democrats are said to be on board with the legislation now, the question is what the sentiment will feel like after November 3. Would polarization only harden after a Democratic rout? What’s the appetite for bipartisan legislation if the election results are contested? That said, there is a strong desire to pass incentives legislation this year, rather than restart the process in the next Congress, when priorities could very well shift.

Getty Images

Cost

Supporters of state tax incentives long have held that the benefits greatly outweigh the costs, but there will be plenty of scrutiny on the bottom line. That typically comes via an analysis from the Congressional Budget Office, so expect to see a lobbying push to outline how the incentive will save or restore jobs.

RELATED: California Governor Frontrunner Xavier Becerra Wants To Save Hollywood, But Offers Few Specifics

A key factor will be whether the ultimate incentive figure is large enough to persuade producers to forgo the UK or Australia or even Canada and locate in the United States. One of the big criticisms of California’s early incentive program was that it was too little, too late, especially with states like New York and Georgia offering much heftier sums of money. Proponents will have to make the case that the incentive will have to be large enough to be meaningful.

Indications are that the bulk of what is being discussed behind closed doors is based in large part on the format and execution of California’s annual program, now at $750 million. A goal of any federal incentive is to snag relocating productions, series or films first made outside the country or content that had already been assured foreign credits but haven’t yet started production.

Jon Voight and Donald Trump Getty Images

Trump

With a few words from his pal Jon Voight, the president threw his support behind an incentive earlier this month, undoubtedly generating some momentum for getting something passed. But he also could change his mind. It’s not out of the realm of possibility that something will trigger him — particularly entertainment-related — that would cause him to shift course.

RELATED Trump Backs Federal Film & TV Tax Incentive: “Hollywood Is A Complete & Total Disaster!”

Among proponents, there’s also a push to highlight support among Republicans, in part to emphasize that the legislation would not just benefit California and New York. That could counterweight the visibility of one of the champions of a federal incentive, California’s junior senator Schiff, one of the president’s biggest foes. He recently told CNN: “Just because it’s this president, if it’s a good idea, I’m not going to oppose it. In fact, I fully support this.”

Asked by Elex Michaelson whether his relationship with the president would make passage more difficult, Schiff said, Schiff noted that Trump has “mentioned bipartisan support, mentioned my support for it, so he didn’t deterred at all by it. He thought that that was a positive.”

The Hollywood factor

The entertainment industry is an easy punching bag, especially on the right, and it’s not hard to see the incentive being cast as a bailout to an elite industry dominated by the left. The Wall Street Journal editorial page quickly weighed in last week, with the headline, “Handouts for Hollywood — Really? Adam Schiff and Donald Trump unite to subsidize the rich and famous.”

“A production tax credit would provide a short-term stimulus for one industry, which primarily supports Democrats,” the Journal‘s editorial team wrote.

RELATED: Illinois Boosts State Film Tax Credit For Environmentally Sustainable Productions

That’s why the support of lawmakers in red states such as Texas, Louisiana and Tennessee might be critical, even with Trump’s backing, as well as the emphasis on legislation as a jobs bill, benefiting an aspect of the manufacturing sector and across different parts of the country.

The Motion Picture Association knows the territory well, as it has sought to make issues like piracy and copyright relevant to the average public whose impressions of the entertainment industry tend toward red carpets and awards show glamour. “The use of the word ‘Hollywood’ has got to stop,” says one booster.

title: Billy Joel Says He Had Brain Surgery After His Diagnosis: ‘Don’t Worry About Me’
summary: Billy Joel says he is doing better after brain surgery helped relieve some of the symptoms of normal pressure hydrocephalus, a disorder he was diagnosed with in 2025. On SiriusXM’s Billy Joel channel Wednesday, the singer talked about the surgery he agreed to after noticing “my balance was not good, I had this sensation of […]
content:
Billy Joel says he is doing better after brain surgery helped relieve some of the symptoms of normal pressure hydrocephalus, a disorder he was diagnosed with in 2025. On SiriusXM’s Billy Joel channel Wednesday, the singer talked about the surgery he agreed to after noticing “my balance was not good, I had this sensation of rocking on a boat.”

The 77-year-old musician revealed in May 2025 that he had been diagnosed with normal pressure hydrocephalus, in which cerebrospinal fluid builds up inside the skull and presses on the brain. He canceled several concerts and said he had been told not to perform until he recovered.

Though he returned in January of this year to perform two songs with a tribute band, he said on Sirius that in general his doctors have asked him not to undergo too much stress.

Popular on Variety

His neurologist said that since it was possible it could continue to get worse, he recommended that Joel have a shunt implanted in his brain. Joel said on Sirius that although he initially didn’t want to have a hole drilled through his brain, after researching it he realized it could help with balance and help memory.

“I don’t want to lose my marbles,” he said. “It’s hard to tell what’s your age and what’s a condition.

“So they implanted a shunt in my brain and it actually improved things. My memory got better, my balance got a little better, my ability to function was better. I realized that because of my job, which is playing rock and roll music very loud, that it was giving me something like a concussion every time I did a show.”

“I’m ok. I want people to know, don’t worry about me. I’m still here,” he assured fans on Wednesday.

title: ‘Jupiter’ Review: A Claustrophobic Study of a Nuclear-Escalation Nightmare That Feels Too Small for the Big Screen
summary: Fictional French President Paul Archambault, as played with gimlet-eyed resolve by Denis Menochet in Alexandre Smia’s “Jupiter” is, we’re cued to believe, a good man. Thrust suddenly into a lurching nuclear crisis, he gathers ministers and advisers around him and listens intently to their staunchly opposing views on escalation vs appeasement. They are also good […]
content:
Fictional French President Paul Archambault, as played with gimlet-eyed resolve by Denis Menochet in Alexandre Smia‘s “Jupiter” is, we’re cued to believe, a good man. Thrust suddenly into a lurching nuclear crisis, he gathers ministers and advisers around him and listens intently to their staunchly opposing views on escalation vs appeasement. They are also good men and good women, cleaving to the same basic humanist principles, while disagreeing volubly on how to put them into practise.

Smia’s film takes a more solemn, less kinetic approach than Kathryn Bigelow’s similarly themed “A House Of Dynamite” but shares its tacit, strangely idealistic faith that the people tasked with thinking through the unthinkable in the event of a nuclear threat, will be dedicated public servants of intelligence and integrity. Given what we know of the world today, the movie’s bid for ruthless realism is slightly undercut by its desire to believe that those whose fingers hover reluctantly over the nuclear button have steady hands.

Popular on Variety

Then again it’s possible that brooding President Archambault only appears to be so selfless because the constricted screenplay (co-written by Smia and Thomas Finkielkraut though there scarcely seems room for two writers) doesn’t give him much self to speak of. As the film begins, Archambault, already ensnared in the tight close-up that DP Nicolas Loir’s relentlessly focussed, somber cinematography will rarely allow him to escape, is receiving some devastating news involving his daughter. It will later be mentioned a couple of times, but this thinly sketched personal tragedy is all the backstory we’ll ever get. Even Archambault’s own political affiliations are kept unspecified.

All we know for sure is that he is on friendly terms with the beleaguered Ukrainian president, Kovalenko. Ukraine is — if you can believe it — in need of military support due to ongoing attacks by Russia, whose premier, Chernov is — don’t know where they got this from — a volatile despot. When Chernov survives an assassination attempt, which was quite likely a false flag operation, he uses the pretext to ramp up the war, and Archambault must decide how far his pledge to protect Ukrainian sovereignty extends. At what point should a nuclear nation intervene, risking its own citizens’ safety, to defend an ally against the aggression of a powerful neighbor? His nominally sympathetic NATO allies refuse to commit to military intervention on the grounds that Ukraine is not a NATO member, so whatever France opts to do, she will be acting unilaterally. Then Chernov detonates an atomic bomb over the Black Sea as a show of force. Archambault and his advisers are moved to the bunker-like war room that gives the film its name. And the nuclear Doomsday clock ticks about twenty seconds closer to midnight.

There’s a prestige-TV-show feel to “Jupiter,” from its economical setting in the same few, featureless interior locations, to the division of the talky action into chapters with ominous headings like “Ultimatum” and “Sacrifice,” to the tension-building score from Olivier Marguerit, which is deployed lavishly over interstitial scenes of Archambault in the back of a car or striding purposefully down a passageway, the weight of the world on his bulky shoulders. The story moves swiftly, as cleanly edited by Pierre Deschamps, but it runs straight rather than deep. Even a fine supporting cast — including Reda Kateb as the hawkish Minister of Defence, Ella Rumpf as a diplomatic adviser and Céline Sallette as French Prime Minister Clara Boyer — are treated more as mouthpieces for various points of view than as actual human beings.

And the insistent focus on Archambault to exclusion of all else does force Menochet’s sober gravitas to do a lot of the heavy lifting in terms of communicating the inner conflict and existential anguish with which all of the team must be struggling. When an aide reports that, with warheads armed and in the air, there are colleagues asking to be allowed take shelter in the bunker, Archambault tells him “Let in as many as you can.” But we never see that process occur, who gets let in and who is denied: as so often, Smia elects to turn away from a potentially emotive dilemma in the name of a paced-up procedural approach that makes “Jupiter” all pulse and no heart.

The situation escalates. The options narrow. After a few futile gambits, global geopolitics devolves from a game of chess to a game of chicken; the only strategy left is choosing whether to blink first without knowing if that blink will be interpreted as the compromise of the wise or the capitulation of the weak. Smia has made an impressively taut debut feature here, but it can feel controlled to a fault, with the iron grip on its grim tone paradoxically betraying a timidity when it comes to exploring the chaos and messiness of human behavior in the face of potential annihilation. As the film smash cuts to black on a frustratingly open-ended, very end-of-episode-one-style cliffhanger, the only conclusion is that in such a hellish scenario, no decision can ever be definitively judged to be the right one. So it’s hard not to feel a little unsatisfied at having just spent 87 minutes watching a man decide.

title: ‘Diarra From Detroit’ Creator Diarra Kilpatrick on the Season 2 Finale, Moving to Paramount+ and Why  Centering Black Women’s Stories Is ‘Inherently Political’
summary: SPOILER ALERT: The following story contains plot details from the Season 2 finale of “Diarra From Detroit” now streaming on Paramount+. With the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger hanging in the balance and a presidential administration that is persistently hostile to diversity, Black-led series like Natasha Rothwell’s well-reviewed Hulu comedy “How to Die Alone,” Issa Rae’s HBO […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: The following story contains plot details from the Season 2 finale of “Diarra From Detroit” now streaming on Paramount+.

With the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger hanging in the balance and a presidential administration that is persistently hostile to diversity, Black-led series like Natasha Rothwell’s well-reviewed Hulu comedy “How to Die Alone,” Issa Rae’s HBO Max series, “Rap Sh*t” and even the NBC drama “Found” have all been given the ax. Black stories are rarely being greenlit on streamers and networks. Still, Paramount+’s “Diarra From Detroit,” a stellar blend of mystery, drama and romance, is shining high in its second season. Yet, the show’s endurance hasn’t been without its challenges. The series, which debuted in 2024 on BET+ to rave reviews, took a two-year hiatus before returning for its second season on Paramount+ this past July. (BET+ was shuttered last spring, with its programming being merged into Paramount+).

​

Created by star and executive producer Diarra Kilpatrick, this season, set amid a classic boiling-hot Detroit summer, finds Diarra trying to find her footing in her newfound relationship with Chris (Shannon Wallace), who is still reeling from his traumatic past. Without a summer school assignment, Diarra decides to use her free time to officially launch her P.I. business. However, being tasked with finding Chris’ uncle’s armoire (which actually turns out to be a desk) leads Diarra, Chris and the school teacher’s best friends Tea (Bryan Terell Clark) and Aja (Dominique Perry) into the underbelly of Detroit, chasing a treasure trove and evading some diabolical gangsters all while trying to iron out all of their personal drama and chaos in between.

​

“We love a gumbo; I love complexity,” Kilpatrick tells Variety. “It pisses me off when work that has a Black woman at the center of it doesn’t respect the audience. We’re not talking about good or bad. That’s a judgment that I’m not interested in. But do you respect the audience? Did you like this woman? I don’t want Black female work to be synonymous with low craftsmanship or low budgets or bad lighting. I want us to be honored. In the medium, in the space. It’s really dawning on me as people are asking me, how does it feel not to be a household name with a whole-ass show at a huge conglomerate where my show is being mentioned in the same breath as ‘Furious’ and ‘Lioness.’ Do you know how much those shows cost to produce? They have some of the biggest stars in the world in them. There was a moment when there was all this niche storytelling happening, and now I’m one of the last people standing.”

​

As “Diarra From Detroit” Season 2 comes to a close, Variety spoke with Kilpatrick about what it took to bring the second season to the small screen, why Black stories matter and her hopes for a possible Season 3.

Paramount+



Season 1 was very winter-coded. Did you always know that you wanted Season 2 to be set in the summer?

When we were shooting in the winter, I started thinking we should probably do a summer season. I think maybe John Chafin, who plays Danger, was like, “Can we move to the summer?” But that was always kind of the plan. I was hoping we would shoot in Detroit proper, and even as a Detroiter, I don’t really want to be in Detroit in the thick of winter. However, when I started writing the pilot, it was literally like the snow took over my body and wrote for me. I was like, “Snow is punishing the city streets.” I think the character was so sad and bereft [following her divorce from Swa, played by Morris Chestnut] that the weather forced itself into the story, externalizing her emotional place when she was really in the winter of her life. So I was very happy to go back to summer. I was also very happy when I saw the special effects budget for adding snow all the damn time. We had a budget cut, so summer felt much cheaper. No coats, no VFXing in snow. So there was that. But I do like the story to unfold in ways that feel like they make sense. I didn’t really know exactly where we would end up, but I knew we were going to come out of that season for her, and it felt fitting to do it in a literal sense as well.

Popular on Variety

Speaking of budget cuts, is that part of the reason why it took so long between the first and second season?

It took them a very long time to pull the trigger on whether they were going to bring the show back. I imagine that had to do with whether they wanted to make the financial commitment. They decided that it would come back, but on a lower budget than Season 1. That impacted where we shot; we moved to Atlanta. It impacted a lot of things, cutting down some regular cast, that kind of thing. Part of it was just the corporate tango of nobody wanting to pull that trigger until the new regime was in place and had given the blessing to do so. We didn’t go into the [writers’] room for a really long time, and then they picked up the room. Then we went into the room, and the room ended, and they still hadn’t picked up the show. So then we were in limbo, waiting.

In Season 2, “Diarra From Detroit” is still at its core an adventure and a mystery, but we also get a thread of romance. Diarra is being pulled between three men: Chris, Royce (Clifford “Method Man” Smith) and Danger. What was it like having a romantic element within the mystery-thriller adventure of it all, but also this thread of motherhood that Diarra is really pondering this entire time?

You really hit the nail on the head with the two things I love to play with in the show: the emotional truths of Black womanhood and the fantasy. We’re in a world now where it seems like nobody can agree on anything, but you know what we can agree on? Method Man is fine. John Chafin is fine. Morris Chestnut is still fine. So if we can’t come together over anything, let’s come together over that. Let’s give people a fantasy every week. I’ve said before, I’ll say it again, I love to see a Black woman at the center of a story, particularly one where she’s the object of desire. I think it’s healing not only for the audience, but it’s also expansive for everybody else to see that and to participate in Black womanhood and all of its glory. It’s a vibe. It’s a good time. Join the party. And I love that, because we hit so many emotional truths in the motherhood conversation; so many of my friends and I are struggling with that, talking about it or figuring it out. Because when we do that, it gives us the grace to go into some more far-fetched places, to go for some bigger laughs and bigger set pieces and to go into some of the fantasy, for the audience to go with us on the fantasy of being romanced by the finest of the fine, of wearing the best clothes, of running around solving a mystery in Detroit and still having your hair laid.

BET/Paramount+



You also weave this beautiful ribbon of history into the show. Audiences learn about bootlegging during Prohibition, the Underground Railroad and quilting and what that has meant for the Black community and the Black church specifically. Is “Diarra From Detroit” a political show?



I would say anytime you put a Black woman in the center of something, it is inherently political in a lot of ways, simply because we just haven’t seen it enough for it to be old hat. People put so much on it. That’s where the fun is. Maybe I’m just a Black nerd, but I have always loved watching movies like “National Treasure” and “The Da Vinci Code.” I love watching a piece of fiction and then going on Google later to be like, “Wait a minute, how much of this is true and how much of these gaps are filled in by the imagination of the writer?” I guess at the end of the day, I’m the daughter of the teacher. So one thing [my mom] did was really instill in me the joy of learning, history and facts. “Indiana Jones,” “National Treasure” — it’s like there are no Black women in these movies. At all. You struggle to find a Black woman who speaks; maybe she has two lines, rolls her neck and then moves on. I really wanted us to write in the very center of that genre. I think the facts give it legitimacy: it was well-researched and brought in some truths about the city. To me, we were kind of just following the genre playbook.



Despite budget cuts and a change in platform, you also had so many people show up for you as guest stars this season, from Nicco Annan to Lovie Simone, Bokeem Woodbine, Lil Rel Howery, Amber Riley, Phylicia Rashad, Morris Chestnut and countless others. What has that meant for you?

As a community, Black Hollywood has a soul. Rel came into my DMs and was like, “I love this show.” When I hit him like, “We’re going to make you an offer,” he was down; he was in. Colman [Domingo] has said publicly that he would work for scale, which I keep repeating. That’s a big deal. It can be scary, because we operate a lot like an independent film. The way we shoot the show, no one gets all kinds of takes. You have to come in, do your thing, hit it and quit it. So there can be a fear in asking really prominent actors to come into a space where we’re going to be moving really quickly. But everybody came ready to play, loving the show, loving their character, and were just down to come in and sprinkle their magic over it. So it does make me emotional, because I was going a thousand miles per hour in the middle of it, just trying to get it done.

Speaking of emotional, in the Season 2 finale, “A Cold Ass Wedding,” Diarra and Aja’s friendship breaks down. Why was that important to illustrate when their bond has been such a glue in the series?

I think Tea and Aja have been [Diarra’s] chosen family, and they’ve really been there for her even when her marriage was breaking down. But Diarra and Aja’s characters have been at real odds, and we’ve played it a lot for the comedy of it. Aja is the voice of reason, and Diarra pushes full throttle ahead. You can’t rob the audience of the inevitable, and it just felt like there was going to be an inevitable tension point between the two of them. Also, Dominique Perry is such a fantastic actress and so funny that I also wanted a chance to see her spread her dramatic wings a little bit there too. It felt inevitable that they’d reach a real impasse and that Aja would break. I don’t know that we know how to move through conflict as friends as well as we do in romantic relationships. So we just wanted to explore that, and we’ll see how their relationship is impacted, hopefully, if we get another season.

Paramount+



​

Speaking of another season, what has it been like to experience the show on Paramount+, which is a much bigger platform than BET+ was?



It’s exciting, in a word — and it’s also complicated. BET+ going away meant a lot of people lost their jobs, and you can imagine that was a lot of Black people because it was at BET+. So you have to hope those people really land on their feet. But, as it relates to the show, I felt really excited about more people having access to this story. I really want to entertain a massive audience, and I want to bring them the nuance and specificity of me, Detroit, my sense of humor, my humanity and my heart. So it does feel like such an opportunity to reach a wider audience. The question is whether that audience will tap in, because I love that the Black audience has been really vocal on Threads, has made their opinions known, and has come to bully me to make sure that Diarra picks the man they like and all of that. But I have also seen people be like, “Wait, how come Paramount+ hasn’t shown me this show?” The algorithms are different, and we are in the echo chamber of our own algorithm, so it takes a little more time for other people to be introduced to the show and to tap in.

title: ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Has Already Made $50 Million in Pre-Sales, Three Months Before Release
summary: Doomsday typically indicates disaster, but for Marvel Studios that term is forecasting a booming box office. Disney reports that the next entry in the sprawling Marvel Cinematic Universe, “Avengers: Doomsday,” has already made $50 million in domestic pre-sales, three months before the movie’s Dec. 18 release date. The studio reported that more than 70% of […]
content:
Doomsday typically indicates disaster, but for Marvel Studios that term is forecasting a booming box office.

Disney reports that the next entry in the sprawling Marvel Cinematic Universe, “Avengers: Doomsday,” has already made $50 million in domestic pre-sales, three months before the movie’s Dec. 18 release date. The studio reported that more than 70% of those pre-sales are for Infinity Vision tickets, emphasizing the audience’s appetite for premium large format screens. “Infinity Vision” is a new certification for premium large format theaters, which Disney unveiled at CinemaCon, touted as delivering “the biggest, brightest and most immersive cinematic experiences” for moviegoers.

The pre-sale figures for “Doomsday” were announced Wednesday by Walt Disney Company senior executive VP & Chief Financial Officer, Hugh Johnston, at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference.

Popular on Variety

Directed by Anthony and Joe Russo, the movie sees a massive assembly of Marvel superheroes, including the Avengers, Fantastic Four, Thunderbolts and the original X-Men, teaming up to face their most formidable foe yet: Victor Von Doom. Robert Downey Jr. returns to play the MCU’s new Big Bad after Tony Stark/Iron Man’s death at the end of “Avengers: Endgame.”

In addition to Downey Jr. returning, Chris Evans is back as Steve Rogers/Captain America after he traveled back in time and stepped away from his superhero duties in “Endgame.” Chris Hemsworth also reprises his role as Thor, alongside Paul Rudd as Ant-Man, Letitia Wright as Black Panther, Sebastian Stan as the Winter Soldier, Tom Hiddleston as Loki and Simu Liu as Shang-Chi.

“Doomsday” also marks the official MCU debut for several of Fox’s past “X-Men” stars after Disney acquired the studio. Patrick Stewart is back as Charles Xavier, Ian McKellen is Magneto, James Marsden is Cyclops, Kelsey Grammer is Beast, Rebecca Romijn is Mystique, Alan Cumming is Nightcrawler and Channing Tatum is Gambit.

The “Fantastic Four: First Steps” stars, comprised of Pedro Pascal as Mister Fantastic, Vanessa Kirby as the Invisible Woman, Joseph Quinn as Human Torch and Ebon Moss-Bachrach as the Thing are back for “Doomsday,” as are the “Thunderbolts” cast, including Florence Pugh as Yelena Belova, David Harbour as Red Guardian, Lewis Pullman as Sentry, Wyatt Russell as U.S. Agent and Hannah John-Kamen as Ghost.

Ahead of the film’s release, Marvel has also launched “Countdown to ‘Avengers: Doomsday‘ Official Podcast.” The podcast covers five films from the Infinity Saga: “The Avengers” (the subject of the podcast’s Aug. 27 debut episode); “Avengers: Age of Ultron” (Sept. 3); “Captain America: Civil War” (Sept. 10); “Avengers: Infinity War” (Sept. 17); and “Avengers: Endgame” (Sept. 24). All five films are available to stream on Disney+. The fifth episode of the podcast will coincide with the Sept. 25, 2026, re-release of “Avengers Endgame: Encore” in theaters.

content:
Heads turned across West Los Angeles this afternoon as smoke rose near the Getty Center.

The fire, which was first spotted shortly after 4 p.m., was burning in the hills near Getty Center Drive in Brentwood. It quickly grew into a five-acre blaze, with first responders on the scene. Additional resources, including LAFD hand crews had been requested.

According to the Watch Duty app, evacuation warnings were issued for two areas of Brentwood at about 4:40 p.m. A Getty Center employee told Deadline that guests were being evacuated and the facility was closed. No structures were threatened, according to officials.
