title: Netflix’s YA Rowing Drama ‘Crew Girl’ Capsizes and Sinks: TV Review
summary: Created by Vivian Lin, Netflix’s latest YA series “Crew Girl” brings audiences into the competitive world of rowing. The show follows 16-year-old Teagan Tao (Miku Martineau), a single sculler whose entire life is derailed after her father, David (Byron Lawson), a wealthy hotelier, is caught stealing money from his clients. When David flees before the […]
content:
Created by Vivian Lin, Netflix’s latest YA series “Crew Girl” brings audiences into the competitive world of rowing. The show follows 16-year-old Teagan Tao (Miku Martineau), a single sculler whose entire life is derailed after her father, David (Byron Lawson), a wealthy hotelier, is caught stealing money from his clients. When David flees before the FBI can arrest him, Teagan and her mother, Ella (Jessica Paré), are blindsided, and are forced to leave their affluent Los Angeles community for Ella’s hometown, Eagle’s Cove, a fictional town in Massachusetts. A series about fresh starts, burgeoning romances and becoming a part of a team, “Crew Girl” is pretty to look at, but its lack of realism, choppy dialogue and monotonous themes sink the show.

​

“Crew Girl” begins with a celebratory moment. With her parents in the audience, Teagan begins her race in the single sculler. Unfortunately, just before she wins, David steps away, leaving a short apology text in his wake just as the FBI swarms the stands. Six months later, having no resources aside from Teagan’s education fund, the mother/daughter pack up their lives and drive East to settle into Ella’s worn childhood home. Though Teagan isn’t thrilled about the transition, she puts her best foot forward at Easton Prep, quickly befriending border Juliet Morny (Olga Petsa) and getting in the crosshairs of Britney Garner (Sage Linder), the school’s resident Regina George.

​

But Teagan’s hopes for a fresh start are dashed when she hears from Coach Matt Hayden (Thomas Cadrot) that Easton Prep has a crew team only for boys. Determined, Teagan bulldozes her way through the boathouse, eventually becoming the team’s coxswain, the only non-rowing member who is tasked with steering, managing the race plan and motivating the rest of the team. To say Teagan has her work cut out for her is an understatement. The eight-man crew consists of rival cousins Josh (Sam Braun) and Ryder Regis (Connor Paton), scholarship student Cam Dillinger (Kyle Clark) and Britney’s twin brother, Bronson “Baloo” Garner (Jude Wilson), among others. The guys initially act like redpill-coded frat bros, and Teagan has to win the boys over so they can start winning races and get the school administration to consider a girls’ team.

​

Across eight episodes, “Crew Girl” does have some redeeming qualities. Casting Martineau (who also stars in Netflix’s “Bet”), a Japanese Canadian, as the lead is an important marker of representation in a genre that rarely puts Black people and people of color in the driver’s seat. Moreover, though most of the adults showcased here are terrible parents who parentify their kids and focus on their own interests, Ella and Teagan’s mother-daughter bond is lovely. It’s built on safety and an appropriate amount of transparency. Moreover, the camaraderie and chemistry between Teagan and her crewmates, especially her respective sparks with both Cam and Josh, give the series some much-needed intrigue. Still, these highlights don’t save “Crew Girl” from falling into the same corny, cookie-cutter narratives we’ve seen countless times.

​

The issues plaguing “Crew Girl” are the same problems that affect other recent YA dramas like Netflix’s “My Life With the Walter Boys” or Prime Video’s “The Runarounds”; the story has no real heart, soul or texture. While the show has all the themes expected in series focused on teenagers and young adults, worn-down tropes hinder “Crew Girl,” leaving its cast to sleepwalk through unrealistic, contrived plot points.

​

As Gen Z and Gen Alpha come of age, they face many of the same things the generations before them had to navigate. Yet, they are the first to be coming into their own at this specific point in history. By highlighting a posh prep school and an all-boys rowing team divided between the haves and have-nots, “Crew Girl” isn’t speaking to a generation dealing with a hyper-digital world, post-pandemic anxiety and so much more.

​

Until creators and writers capture the specificity of this time, audiences will be doomed to watch regurgitated stories that don’t highlight the uniqueness of Gen Z and how they are engaging with the world. Millennials and Gen X can look back in the zeitgeist of television and see their adolescence immortalized; young people today deserve the same reverence.

“Crew Girl” is now streaming on Netflix.

title: Elon Musk Embarks On Vicious Rant About “Bitter Old Man” Alex Gibney & Threatens To Sue Over ‘Musk’ Documentary
summary: Elon Musk has gone on an hours-long rampage about Alex Gibney after the Oscar-winning director premiered his documentary about the tech mogul at the Venice Film Festival. In a series of vicious and sometimes bizarre posts on X/Twitter, Musk accused the filmmaker of having “zero integrity” and being a “bitter old man who lost the […]
content:
Elon Musk has gone on an hours-long rampage about Alex Gibney after the Oscar-winning director premiered his documentary about the tech mogul at the Venice Film Festival.

In a series of vicious and sometimes bizarre posts on X/Twitter, Musk accused the filmmaker of having “zero integrity” and being a “bitter old man who lost the plot long ago.”

Musk accused “horrible human” Gibney of directing a “hit piece that misses” in the shape of Musk, adding that the movie was “boring af [as f***]” because it is four hours long.

Representatives for Musk and Gibney have been contacted for comment.

Watch on Deadline

Delving into conspiracies, Musk alleged that the film was a “psy op” and shared an image purporting to show that Gibney was being puppeteered by the Democrats and George Soros.

He also shared an image of Gibney with a realistic poop emoji on his head. “It’s an improvement,” he laughed.

More specifically, Musk took issue with the claims of Ashley St. Clair, the conservative influencer who bore a son by Musk in 2024.

The Tesla boss denied that she was offered a $40 million financial settlement after their split that would have required her to sign a non-disclosure agreement. “She was never offered that and has a history of making false claims,” Musk wrote.

He has also reportedly threatened to sue Gibney’s production company Jigsaw Productions over the documentary’s suggestion that Musk used his Starlink satellites to influence the 2024 U.S. election in favor of Donald Trump.

The New York Post cited a legal letter from Musk’s attorney Alex Spiro, in which the lawyer wrote: “You are … on notice, before release, that the insinuation is false, that the material refuting it is public, and that you chose not to be told the rest.”

According to reports on Musk amid its Venice screening, St. Clair said in the movie: “He had told me [before the election] he was going to unleash the ‘anomaly in the matrix.’”

“Starlink was not connected to vote tabulation. Election officials in multiple states, independent cybersecurity researchers, and fact-checkers publicly refuted the Starlink vote-rigging claim in November 2024, and nothing since has revived it,” Spiro reportedly wrote.

Speaking at a Venice Film Festival press conference, Gibney said he encountered a “tremendous sense of fear” as he canvassed for interviewees for the film.

“What I discovered was that the story of Musk was not, in a way, a new tech story. Though there’s much about it that is tech, but… his story is really the story of an old wine in a new bottle. His story turns out to be the story of the confidence man, the stock pumper, his wealth and power comes from inflated stock, and so I had told that story before with Enron and with Elizabeth Holmes, and so it was a story that was oddly familiar to me,” said Gibney.

title: Paul Mescal, Tracy Letts & Uzo Aduba Among Names Set For National Theatre Productions In 2027
summary: The National Theatre in London has set its 2027 lineup, with Tracy Letts and Uzo Aduba among the actors making their debut at the venue, and Paul Mescal among the returning performers.  Letts will perform alongside Mescal in a rep production of Arthur Miller’s Death of a Salesman, directed by Rebecca Frecknall in the National’s […]
content:
The National Theatre in London has set its 2027 lineup, with Tracy Letts and Uzo Aduba among the actors making their debut at the venue, and Paul Mescal among the returning performers.

Letts will perform alongside Mescal in a rep production of Arthur Miller’s Death of a Salesman, directed by Rebecca Frecknall in the National’s Lyttelton Theatre. The production will be held in the summer and autumn of 2027. Further cast joining Mescal and Letts include Peter Corboy, Eimhin Fitzgerald Doherty, Ryan Donaldson, Ciarán Hinds, Aisling Loftus, Julian Moore-Cook, and Monica Dolan.

Alongside Death of a Salesman, Mescal will also perform in a summer/autumn 2027 production of Tom Murphy’s A Whistle in the Dark at the National. Caitríona McLaughlin will direct the production. Following its run at the National Theatre, A Whistle in the Dark will play at Ireland’s Abbey Theatre from 13 – 30 October 2027, as part of the Dublin Theatre Festival.

Watch on Deadline

Aduba is set to make her National debut in The Adeyemis – A Family Saga, written by Oladipo Agboluaje. The production will be held in winter 2027 in the Dorfman Theatre. The new play follows the fortunes of a wealthy but troubled clan through a turbulent period in Nigeria’s recent history. Lucian Msamati is set to direct.

Elsewhere, Emma Corrin will star in a revival of Tennessee Williams’s Suddenly Last Summer alongside Harriet Walter. Michael Grandage will direct the production, while Richard Eyre will direct a new production of David Hare’s Plenty.

Dear England and Ink scribe James Graham will also debut a new production titled Major. It will be directed by Jeremy Herrin. The play is said to explore the pivotal moment when John Major took over from Margaret Thatcher.

title: The Sidemen Rep Arcade Signs Max Fosh, Friends From Work & More Ahead Of Europe’s First Creator Upfront
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Arcade, the management company of The Sidemen, has signed a host of creators, as it relaunches as an entertainment business ahead of its first European upfront. Comedian Max Fosh, creator collective Friends From Work (comprising Arthur Frederick, Arthur Hill, George Clarkey and ItalianBach), John Nellis, Faith Kelly, Generation Football and Fallow Chefs have all […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Arcade, the management company of The Sidemen, has signed a host of creators, as it relaunches as an entertainment business ahead of its first European upfront.

Comedian Max Fosh, creator collective Friends From Work (comprising Arthur Frederick, Arthur Hill, George Clarkey and ItalianBach), John Nellis, Faith Kelly, Generation Football and Fallow Chefs have all signed with Arcade. The Sidemen, who recently saw member KSI exit, will continue with Arcade as well.

The new focus is turning Europe’s most popular and active creators into media brands that operate across content, commerce and culture, with IP development becoming a more central part of the mix.

Jack Croft & Will Murray, who co-founded upmarket London restaurant Fallow and run the Fallow Chefs channel, said: “We built Fallow by ripping up the rulebook – and we’ve tried to do the same with everything we post. Signing with Arcade makes sense because it’s a team built by creators, for creators, that lives and breathes the creator economy the way we live and breathe restaurants. We’re thrilled to be joining forces – we’ve got a lot of ambitious ideas, and now we’ve got the right people to help us pull them off.”

Watch on Deadline

Next Thursday, Arcade is hosting Europe’s first creator media upfront at an invite-only event in London. This is expected to attract over 150 advertisers, brands and partners businesses, who will get exclusive previews of creator content slates, audience data and insights – similar to the U.S. NewFronts.

This comes after Arcade received a seven-figure investment from Lumina Media, and hired former Vice exec Matt Elek as CEO, with co-founder Jordan Schwarzenberger stepping away from the day-to-day running of the company, while retaining an active role.

“Arcade is executing an ambitious growth strategy to become the dominant player in the creator economy in Europe, which is demonstrated by our incredible new line-up of creator media partners,” said Elek. “We’ve built the entertainment company that creators actually need, and the wider market is only now starting to catch up.”

Besides its management arm, Arcade has a commercial business that works on partnerships with the likes of Virgin Media O2, Formula E and Unilever, while its advertising division, Creator Access, has a YouTube Partner Sales license, which it says guarantees ad sales against its creative talent. Joe Lamb is Arcade’s Commercial Managing Director, and Adam Smith leads the Creator Access division.

“Creators aren’t just building channels anymore, they’re building entire media brands — long-form, IP, live, branded entertainment” said Schwarzenberger. “Arcade gives our partners access to the biggest creator media brands in Europe, which operate with the same scale and sophistication as a broadcaster or streamer, but with the trust and audience reach only these elite creators have.”

Schwarzenberger, Sam Uwins and Aaron O’Neill co-founded Arcade in 2021 as the management and ventures company for YouTube’ creator group giants The Sidemen. Lumina has a minority stake in the business, as Thomas Benski seeks to build a portfolio of investments, including in Carrousel Studios, Strike, Wayward Films, Creators Corp, Magna Studios and Arcade.

Benski, founder and CEO of Lumina, said: “We invested in Arcade because we believe they have the team, talent and ambition to build one of the defining companies in the creator economy. They’ve already built something special. Our role is to give Jordan, Matt and the team the backing, network leverage, growth company experience and resources to take that ambition to the next level, and we’re incredibly excited about what they can build from here.”

title: ‘RuPaul’s Drag Race UK’ Canceled By BBC Amid “Financial Pressures”
summary: RuPaul’s Drag Race UK has reached the end of the runway on the BBC. The BBC has decided not to renew Drag Race UK beyond Season 8 this year, citing “financial pressures” as the UK broadcaster seeks savings of £500 million ($677 million). Producer World of Wonder plans to pivot the show, as well as […]
content:
RuPaul’s Drag Race UK has reached the end of the runway on the BBC.

The BBC has decided not to renew Drag Race UK beyond Season 8 this year, citing “financial pressures” as the UK broadcaster seeks savings of £500 million ($677 million).

Producer World of Wonder plans to pivot the show, as well as spin-off series, to its streaming service, Wow Presents Plus, promising a “new era” for the franchise.

A BBC spokesperson said: “As the BBC continues to navigate significant financial pressures and deliver the savings required of us, we have had to make some very difficult choices, none of which have been taken lightly.

“We can therefore confirm together with World of Wonder, that RuPaul’s Drag Race UK will be leaving the BBC and moving to Wow Presents Plus. The BBC is incredibly proud of all eleven series of this groundbreaking show and we would like to thank RuPaul, World of Wonder and everyone involved, both on and off screen.”

Watch on Deadline

Featuring judges RuPaul, Michelle Visage, Graham Norton and Alan Carr, Drag Race has averaged around 1.5 million viewers, according to BBC News.

Drag Race UK is the latest show to fall victim to cuts after the BBC canceled Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, and Live At The Apollo in July.

title: UK Industry Program Breakthrough Leaders Widens Focus To International Biz & Becomes Global Breakthrough 360
summary: EXCLUSIVE: British industry initiative Breakthrough Leaders is expanding globally. The UK leadership program for individuals from Black, Asian and Global Majority backgrounds is evolving into Global Breakthrough 360 (GB360) as a response to the increasingly international nature of television. The new evolution of Breakthrough Leaders will place focus on Africa and Canada to open routes […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: British industry initiative Breakthrough Leaders is expanding globally.

The UK leadership program for individuals from Black, Asian and Global Majority backgrounds is evolving into Global Breakthrough 360 (GB360) as a response to the increasingly international nature of television.

The new evolution of Breakthrough Leaders will place focus on Africa and Canada to open routes to markets, networks and relationships beyond the UK, to equip its cohorts with understandings of international financing, co-production and cross-border partnerships.

The international collabs are with MIP Africa and the Canada Media Fund. The MIP partnership will see the 2026/27 cohort travel to South Africa for a supported market visit, meeting creators, buyers, distributors and financiers from across the continent. The pact with the Canada Media Fund will aim to build connections between UK and Canadian talent and industry networks.

Watch on Deadline

Alongside this international access, participants will build relationships with senior leaders and decision-makers across the sector, develop their own Personal Board of Advisors, and take part in Leadership Integration Labs led by creative leadership advisor and entrepreneur Rémy Blumenfeld — turning programme insights into practical action and networks that extend far beyond the programme’s 12 months.

The GB360 calendar will also include a new December event at a “landmark central London venue,” which is a first for the program.

A new advisory board comprises Katra Simaball of The Akuna Group, the global creative, entertainment and media company founded by Sir Idris Elba; Tshepiso Sello Chikapa Phiri, founder and CEO of one of South Africa integrated media firm Known Associates Group; Fred Bhat, who leads YouTube, gaming and creator content at the BBC; Tim Yaw Struthers, Head of Original Brands & International Marketing at Sky and Senior Advisor, Global Engagement at The National Film Authority of Ghana; Deep Sehgal, a doc maker and creative director who formerly led Motion WPP Entertainment’s Diverse Indies Fund partnership; Tamara Howe of 22Summers, Elba’s production company; and Sara Putt, talent agent and founder of Sara Putt Associates.

Fremantle will continue as a founding partner of Breakthrough Leaders, with ITV and ITV Studios, Channel 4 and 5 all returning to the program.

The 2026/27 Global Breakthrough 360 cohort will comprise 50 places available, with applications open through a dedicated website before closing on September 18.

Since it began in 2020, Breakthrough Leaders has seen more than 250 senior creatives join its program. Many have gone on to land decision-making roles, and the org says earlier cohorts delivered a 30% promotion rate. Around 32% of previous cohorts are now hiring or championing others for more senior roles, with 68% of alums citing access to decision makers is the single biggest obstacle to career progression. This has directly influenced the decision to sharpen GB360’s focus on networks, visibility and opportunity.

Breakthrough Leaders founder Simone Pennant, who is also behind The TV Collective, received a BAFTA Television Craft Special Award for her contribution to the industry earlier this year off the back of her work with the program.



“Television, film, digital, gaming, podcasting, brands — these worlds no longer operate in silos, and neither do the leaders shaping them,” said Pennant. “Bringing these industries together widens the pool of opportunity and talent alike, creating collaborations that wouldn’t otherwise exist. GB360 connects people, sectors and markets with a real reason to work together — so leaders don’t just adapt to change, they help shape it.”

Ben Frow, Chief Content Officer at 5, said the launch of Global Breakthrough 360 “rightly recognises the shifts in the creative economy and the importance of nurturing business relationships across borders and sectors to deliver innovative new projects,” while Tim Carter, MD of ITV Studios, UK Unscripted added that “creativity and diversity are two sides of the same coin,” and said: “Supporting Breakthrough 360’s excellent programme is about future-proofing our industry.”

Sam Tatlow, Head of DEI at ITV, said it had “never been more important for us all to be working together to ensure we develop the leaders of colour of the future, creating a more representative, creative and inclusive industry for us all.”

Neila Butt, Creative Equity Lead at Channel 4, said the program “was making a real difference to the careers of Black and Asian creatives,” while Lisa Hardy, People Director at Fremantle UK, called GB360 “an important evolution of Breakthrough Leaders.”

title: Dreamkite Chief Yoko Higuchi-Zitzmann on AI Opportunities and Industry Concerns: ‘AI Production Will Create a Lot of New Human Jobs’
summary: Earlier today, Variety announced that international media executive and producer Yoko Higuchi-Zitzmann and AI filmmaker Mark Wachholz have launched Dreamkite Studios, an AI production company. We spoke to Higuchi-Zitzmann about the venture. Are the projects on your slate short-form or will you also be working on feature-length films and series?We’d like to start with short-form […]
content:
Earlier today, Variety announced that international media executive and producer Yoko Higuchi-Zitzmann and AI filmmaker Mark Wachholz have launched Dreamkite Studios, an AI production company. We spoke to Higuchi-Zitzmann about the venture.

Are the projects on your slate short-form or will you also be working on feature-length films and series?

We’d like to start with short-form [content], but we would also like to develop feature films and series because what is not possible now will be possible in four months, and what is not possible in four months will be possible in eight months. The development is so super quick. I’ve been in the business for 20 years, and have a network with the best storytellers, screenwriters and directors. We want to be ready for the next step.

Where do you see the opportunities for AI production?

I think in the fields of animation and advertising, business is already there. But in the long term, you can also produce long feature films and series with AI and hybrid. For example, you have your actors, but if you have a huge action film or huge fantasy film or animation, you could not finance it from Europe in the past. But now we have the possibility to finance with AI big projects in a hybrid system with real actors, but you don’t have to go to the Himalaya mountains or build a huge set in New Zealand for a fantasy film. You can do it with AI. So there are big possibilities for feature films and series, and it’s a huge opportunity also for Europe.

Popular on Variety

How will you distribute your projects?

With disruptive content, you also have to think about disruptive distribution. I think it’s important to be open-minded. Now you have these new elements of distribution like going directly through an app on mobile devices or going directly via YouTube to the customers and finance it through advertisements, or maybe build our own platform, and so on. So, I really respect the traditional world, and I feel privileged to be in this network, and I would love to work with broadcasters and streamers and big distribution companies, but also to have this opportunity to think out of the box, not only in terms of content but also in terms of distribution.

How do you overcome the concerns about AI production?

I think there is a lot of insecurity and fear, which I can really understand, but AI production will create a lot of new human jobs, and I think creatives who really embrace the new technology will be very successful in the future.

I can understand the fear and the insecurity, but my suggestion is to use AI as a tool and a technology to make great human-created content.

title: Ella Langley Leads 2026 CMA Awards Nominations With Nine, as Miranda Lambert, Kacey Musgraves Also Score Big Tallies
summary: In perhaps the least surprising development in recent CMA Awards history, Ella Langley emerged at the front of the pack when nominations for the 2026 telecast were announced Thursday morning, scoring nine in all, just one shy of the all-time single-year record set by Alan Jackson in 2002. Miranda Lambert has this year second-most nominations, […]
content:
In perhaps the least surprising development in recent CMA Awards history, Ella Langley emerged at the front of the pack when nominations for the 2026 telecast were announced Thursday morning, scoring nine in all, just one shy of the all-time single-year record set by Alan Jackson in 2002.

Miranda Lambert has this year second-most nominations, with seven. Some are for her own releases, but it’s notable that four of Lambert’s nods come for her work as a songwriter or producer on recordings by… Ella Langley.

Others being rewarded by Country Music Association voters with multiple nominations include Kacey Musgraves and Ben West with five each; Cody Johnson, Chris Stapleton and Stephen Wilson Jr. with four each; and Lainey Wilson, Luke Combs and Dave Clauss with three nominations each.

Popular on Variety

Foremost among Langley’s nine nods is her first-tine nomination for the CMAs’ top prize, entertainer of the year. Given that Langley has the biggest hit of the year in any genre with “Choosin’ Texas,” a smash that helped propel her to arena headliner status, she has to be considered a frontrunner for the top prize despite this being her first time landing in that rarefied territory.

This marks the first time in three years that two women have been simultaneously nominated for that award, with defending champion Lainey Wilson also earning another shot at it. (Wilson, who picked up EOTY in 2023 and again in 2025, was also announced last week as host for the CMAs telecast for the third year in a row.)

The other three candidates for entertainer of the year are Luke Combs, Cody Johnson and Chris Stapleton. The list of candidates for the top prize duplicates last year’s roster of EOTY nominees, with the exception of Langley taking the spot that went to Morgan Wallen in 2024.

Although he remains undeniably country’s biggest modern superstar, Wallen takes a lower profile in this year’s nods with just two nominations, both of them for collaborations that got nods in the musical event category, including a duet with (surprise) Langley. It was just two years ago that Wallen won entertainer of the year, but his not showing up for the ceremony to claim country music’s highest annual honor may have affected how voters felt about honoring him as EOTY going forward. But it’s also worth noting that, as recordings go, he was off-cycle, with his “I’m the Problem” album predating the 2026 eligibility period and his latest single, “Been by Now,” too fresh to have been considered.

Pop’s biggest superstar, Taylor Swift, returned to her CMA-winning roots by getting a nomination for “I Knew it, I Knew You” for single of the year. It is her first nomination in that category since 2013, when she was nominated for top single for a featured appearance on Tim McGraw’s “Highway Don’t Care.” It is only her second CMA nomination this decade, the last having been for video of the year in 2022 for “I Bet You Think About Me,” a duet with Chris Stapleton. It’s the first stop in what looks to be a long awards season for “I Knew It, I Knew You,” the country-flavored closing theme song from “Toy Story 5,” which is likely to figure into upcoming Grammys and Oscars consideration.

If you’re looking at who has the most increased profile in CMA nominations this year, that would be Stephen Wilson Jr., who last year had just one nomination — for best new artist — even though he was given a big look with repeat appearances on the 2025 telecast. This year, he returns with four nominations, including another shot at best new artist, plus his entree into the coveted male vocalist of the year category.

Langley will compete against herself in one of the marquee categories, single of the year, as she is nominated not just for “Choosin’ Texas” but its followup hit, “Be Her.” Most of the time, artists might be worried about splitting their vote, but “Choosin’ Texas” losin’ any of the the CMAs it’s up for seems like the least likely possibility in a world of theoretical outcomes, as anyone with a song positioned against it this year can consider themselves happy just to be nominated.

“The 60th Annual CMA Awards” airs live Nov. 18 from Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena on ABC and Disney+, with next-day streaming on Hulu.
