content:
Sebastian Stan has been running around the city of Toronto.

We’re sitting in a restaurant, having lunch between his multiple studio visits for various publications. It’s busy and bustling around us, the way TIFF tends to transform every hotel and restaurant over its 11-day period. Stan settles in at the table and digs into a chicken salad. He’s here to talk with Variety about the movie he says he’s been chasing, in one form or another, since he was a teenager.

“Fjord” is the film Stan long promised himself he would make: a return, however partial, to the country he left as a boy and the language he grew up speaking.

Popular on Variety

Directed by Romanian auteur Cristian Mungiu — a filmmaker Stan says he had tracked for years — it is Mungiu’s first English-language feature and Stan’s first Romanian-language role, a project the two circled for a long time before the right script surfaced. Stan plays Mihai, a fundamentalist father whose children are seized by the state, in a story inspired by a real family and shot in Mungiu’s signature register of long, unbroken takes and a pointed refusal of the close-up.

Coming off an Oscar nomination for the drama “The Apprentice” in 2024, the same year he won a Golden Globe for lead actor (comedy) for another movie, “A Different Man,” Stan sees clearly what he’s after and why. He’s a dad now. He has entered his 40s and it has changed him. “How do I raise kids in today’s world?” he asks, flipping the entire interview into a conversation as we eat and drink at the table. “And how do I not pass on something I’m myself trying to work through?”

Stan has become the rare Marvel actor with a foot in the DC world, too. He met “The Batman” filmmaker Matt Reeves, who he said had seen and loved “The Apprentice” and around the same time cold-called DC Studios co-CEO James Gunn to let him know he was available and, in his words, “ready to rock” when the opportunity presented itself. Of course, he won’t confirm his role and the light visibly goes out of his face when the name Harvey Dent, whom he is rumored to be playing, comes up. But he does not undersell what Reeves is building. “I go to set sometimes and I look around and I’m like, I think we’re making fucking ‘Godfather Part Two,’” Stan says of the movie, which he says Reeves has spent three years shaping. “I really don’t want to raise it up, but I do feel like it’s going to be a payoff.”

He calls himself “allergic” to repeating himself and worries that actors have grown too overexposed to disappear into anything. “We’re not doctors, we’re not on the front lines,” he says of why the subject has to matter. “This is the only way we get to communicate.”

“Fjord,” whose reactions on social media have included people branding it “a MAGA movie,” Stan says, has been labeled that by “people who never see it.” He’s hoping this divided country can still sit together in one theater. Whether audiences take him up on it is another question entirely.

“Fjord” is a rare role that lets you speak your mother tongue and work with a filmmaker from home. What did it stir in you to go back?

The movie’s big theme is the immigrant experience, and that was my way in. When I read the script, I remembered coming to the U.S. and the shame I felt — the self-awareness of just being different. My mom always told me, not too dissimilar from this family in the movie, you don’t want to make allies, you don’t want to make enemies, you want to be nice to everybody. As I got older and got more confident about embracing my differences, around 16, 17, I told myself I had to go back and find a movie to do in Romania one day, to reconnect. Cristian was one of the filmmakers I’d been tracking. I knew how he shot, how morally ambiguous he liked to make his films. We kept trying to find the right thing, and finally he called and said, “I think I have this movie. It’ll be my first English-language movie and your first Romanian movie.” It was a good fit.

The film is inspired by a real family whose children are taken by the state. Where do you draw the line between honoring what happened and finding your own Mihai?

We looked at that particular family, but Cristian was adamant that we not focus on them entirely, because a lot of the movie is still fictional. So I looked at a lot of different families — and I looked at my own. I had a very particular relationship with my father, and I also grew up with my grandfather on my mom’s side. I had that stereotypical Eastern European father — this more subdued, stern, not-so-readable, guarded presence — and I think that informed a lot of my choices. But this family has a specific belief system. We went to some sermons in Romania to get a sense of the religion, and there’s an inherent trust that, no matter how things go, God will reveal that everything will be OK. That was very contrary to how I would react if my kids were taken from me.

You’ve talked about difficult relationships with your father — and gave a shoutout to your stepdad in your Golden Globe speech for “A Different Man,” who raised you. Now that you’re a father, do you feel a responsibility or a subconscious redemption arc?

I think some of it is, ‘Oh, I’ll right the wrongs I couldn’t when I was living my own experience’ — I can maybe provide the things I didn’t have. But mostly I’m more mindful. You start to realize how much of our parents and the voices in our heads are things we took on growing up, not necessarily authentically us. How do I manage that, so I don’t pass on something I’m myself still trying to work through?

The reactions to “Fjord” have been divisive, and I’ve read some that have called it ‘A MAGA movie.’ How do you feel about that?

Here’s the thing: When did it become normalized to think that one side has all the answers and is completely faultless? A lot of those reactions come from people who haven’t seen the movie. It highlights why we need more films like this — to remind us there was a time when people could meet, disagree and at least hear each other out. The movie doesn’t go and point the finger and say, “Well, you hold the key and you don’t.” It’s just going, “Fuck, we’re flawed as people.” And, by the way, kids shouldn’t be the ones paying the price for that.

I also read somewhere that people wanted to see your character explode. He never quite does.

In real life, people don’t always have the tools for that. Coming off “A Different Man” and “The Apprentice,” where I played these larger-than-life characters, I wanted something difficult in a different direction. I knew Cristian likes to shoot these long one-takes; I knew he doesn’t like close-ups and it was a different challenge to do something more restrained — something that reminded me of the unpredictability I saw in men who don’t know how to express themselves. Movies sometimes make that a little more romantic.

Coming off an Oscar nomination for “The Apprentice,” and no shade to any of your MCU counterparts, but you’re one of the only people using your post-MCU powers for good — a stretch nobody would call safe. What are you chasing in a role now that you weren’t a few years ago?

One, I’m chasing the opportunity to offer something different. I’ve become allergic to repeating myself. Actors are so overexposed at this point — whether you’re on social media or not, everything is personal, everyone wants to know everything. It makes the job harder, because people want to see you play one thing. I don’t care as much what it is, as long as it lets me offer something new. If that’s paired with a topic that’s relevant, it becomes even more undeniable. As you get older, you want to do something that can stand the test of time, that’s a conversation starter about the relevant issues we’re dealing with. We’re not doctors; we’re not on the front lines. This is the only way we get to communicate.

Did you grow up watching Batman? And did you ever think you’d be in a Batman movie?

100%. My favorite superhero movie is “Batman Returns” — I remember exactly where I saw it, over Christmas. I didn’t see the original first. It was Michelle Pfeiffer, Danny DeVito and I was obsessed with that movie. I also, shamefully, really like “Batman Forever” — I love the Riddler, I love Jim Carrey …

What about Tommy Lee Jones?

[pauses] He’s an amazing actor. I don’t quite know. In that movie, Jim Carrey overshadowed him.

Interesting.

But, growing up in Europe, Batman was the most recognizable thing to me. So when the MCU came first, it opened a door to comics I didn’t grow up with and I thought, well, that’s it, there’s no way I can get to the other side. No one’s going to hire me; I’ll be Bucky.

And then …?

Two things happened at the same time. I got a call to go meet Matt Reeves, who had seen “The Apprentice” and loved it and said, “I want to talk to you about this new movie.” And at the same time, I’d reached out to James Gunn and said, “Listen, man, I’m just letting you know — I’m here, I’m alive and well, I’m ready to rock.” And then it happened. I still feel like sometimes I’m like, did I leave the team for the other team? These worlds keep going parallel, and weirdly they help each other.

Everyone’s asking you about Harvey Dent. There was a video of you basically walking away from the question. Do you have newfound respect for Tom Holland when it comes to secrecy?

I have a lot of respect for Tom Holland. He was always notoriously bad at it, right? Look, there’s no way to keep any secret anymore. What I’ll say is this: there’s no way people will fully grasp how this movie is until they see it. I go to set sometimes and I look around and I’m like, I think we’re making fucking “The Godfather Part Two.” I feel that highly about it. Matt has spent three years working on it. There’s a lot of speculation about these roles, about what this movie is, but I think it’s going to be a good payoff — it’s really grounded and real, and that’s what I loved about it. You want to tease it a little, but we still have a long time.

Last question. David Harbour did this when I sat down with him — can you say one line from the movie, out of context, that your character says?

What did David say?

His was “You … are Tony Stark.”

That’s tricky. Ummm …

Do you say ‘Hello’ or anything like that?

I don’t even know if I say “hello.” [laughs] I want to give you something good. Let me say that the word “cookies” comes up. So enjoy that.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

title: ‘Onwards and Sideways’ Director John Madden on Returning to TIFF After 16 Years With His Parkinson’s Romantic Drama Starring Laura Linney and Rhys Ifans
summary: When director John Madden first read Paul Mayhew-Archer’s script that was based on his experience living with Parkinson’s disease, he knew it had a ways to go. But he recognized its potential. Now nearly a decade later, Madden is ready to show “Onwards and Sideways” to buyers at the Toronto Intl. Film Festival. What initially […]
content:
When director John Madden first read Paul Mayhew-Archer’s script that was based on his experience living with Parkinson’s disease, he knew it had a ways to go. But he recognized its potential.

Now nearly a decade later, Madden is ready to show “Onwards and Sideways” to buyers at the Toronto Intl. Film Festival. What initially started as a “boy meets girl” script evolved into something much more complicated, Madden says, now beginning with a chance encounter as two strangers are diagnosed with Parkinson’s on the same morning at the same hospital.

“That opened up a different kettle of fish,” Madden tells Variety. “It ended up being much more involving than one had anticipated.”

Popular on Variety

The story follows the ripple effects of that chance encounter between Tony (Rhys Ifans) and Emma (Laura Linney), a teacher and composer who find their lives forever intertwined as they take in the news that they only have “five good years” left to live, per their blunt neurologist. “Onwards and Sideways” follows the pair over the course of five chapters as they fall in love and change each other’s lives after Tony reluctantly takes up Emma’s suggestion on joining a Parkinson’s ballet class.

While much remains unknown about the disease, including the cause, over 10 million people are estimated to be living with Parkinson’s around the world, according to the Parkinson’s Foundation. It’s a disorder of the nervous system that restricts movement across the body, and the effects are felt more over time.

“Most of us, in some way or another, are a degree or two of separation away from the condition,” Madden says. “You don’t have to go very far before you bump into that.”

Madden spent time working with both Ifans and Linney separately, and describes their chemistry as “natural” when they began rehearsing scenes together.

“The way they respond to one another was fantastic, particularly given that they were acting completely out of chronological order and working with a condition that actually had to be minutely calibrated from moment to moment,” Madden says.

Two consultants worked closely on the film and ensured that its depiction of Parkinson’s was authentic. That was especially important for Rhys and Linney, who portray characters with different symptoms.

“Very quickly, it became natural, instinctive,” Madden adds.

But while “Onwards and Sideways” is bringing Madden back to TIFF after 16 years, where he previously unspooled “The Debt” and “Proof,” it’s a noticeably different strategy than 1998‘’’s “Shakespeare in Love” employed, which put him on the map with a director Oscar nomination while the film won best picture.

“We weren’t in a position to go the festival route because [distributor Miramax] wanted to get it out before the end of the year,” Madden says, recalling the film’s effective late-year release strategy. “I said to [then Miramax topper] Harvey Weinstein, ‘Look, whatever we do, you can’t let people watch this with four or five people in a screening room. You have to put it with an audience.’ So we played it at the Paris Theater [in New York] and that was it.”

As Madden hops on a plane to Toronto, bringing “Onwards and Sideways” directly to audiences to see how they respond, he looks back on getting to collaborate with Mayhew-Archer and commends the BAFTA nominee’s “defiance” in living with Parkinson’s.

“He doesn’t belabor his own condition,” Madden says. “He’s on record as saying it’s one of the best things that ever happened to him.”

title: ‘Obsession’ One Year Later: Inde Navarrette and Curry Barker Dish on Memes, How Nikki Became More ‘Flirty’ and Their Wild Ride at TIFF
summary: “Obsession’s” origin story is the stuff of legend. On Sept. 7, 2025, just two days after its rapturously received premiere in the Midnight Madness section of the Toronto International Film Festival, distributor Focus Features offered to acquire its rights for $14-$15 million. The film, about a friend-zoned record store employee named Bear (Michael Johnston) who […]
content:
“Obsession’s” origin story is the stuff of legend.

On Sept. 7, 2025, just two days after its rapturously received premiere in the Midnight Madness section of the Toronto International Film Festival, distributor Focus Features offered to acquire its rights for $14-$15 million. The film, about a friend-zoned record store employee named Bear (Michael Johnston) who forces the object of his desire, Nikki (Inde Navarrette), to fall madly — and I do mean madly — in love with him via a mystical toy, was released the following May, where it became a cultural phenomenon, grossing over $500 million worldwide (against a $750,000 budget) and vaulting its 26-year-old writer-director, Curry Barker, and star Inde Navarrette, 25, to the top of the Hollywood A-list. Barker subsequently signed an eight-figure deal with Universal and Blumhouse, who helped shepherd “Obsession,” for his third feature, while Navarrette was cast as Rogue in Marvel’s “X-Men” reboot.

A little over a year after its world premiere, on Friday, Barker and Navarrette returned to TIFF, the place where their lives changed, for a discussion titled “DIALOGUES The ‘Obsession’ Obsession with Curry Barker & Inde Navarrette” at the John Bassett Theatre as part of its inaugural industry-focused hub TIFF: The Market. And to say it was a hot ticket would be an understatement: An hour before showtime, the line for the talk snaked all the way down and around the halls of the Metro Toronto Convention Centre housing the theater.

Popular on Variety

“What a difference a year makes!” declared TIFF Midnight Madness programmer Peter Kuplowsky, who moderated the talk. Barker and Navarrette regaled the packed theater with how wild the past year and change has been.

Barker, who’d risen to prominence acting and directing in YouTube videos, opened up about how he wanted to become “a true storyteller” and thus opted not to act in “Obsession,” unlike most of his other work. Meanwhile, Navarrette dished on how she was drawn to the project because it was the polar opposite of the type of work she’d done before in shows like “13 Reasons Why” and “Superman & Lois.”

“I got sent the script because I wanted to do something completely different than I’d ever done before,” she said. “I had this fire in my belly, and I wanted to show people what I could do.”

Navarrette sent in a self-tape for “Obsession” and was convinced it didn’t go well.

“I thought I bombed it,” she maintained, “but then I was lucky enough that he saw something in me that I didn’t feel like I had shown.”

Chemistry reads with Johnston followed, where she felt more confident in her ability to bring Nikki to life. And the very first day of shooting was the bedroom scene where Nikki freaks out while kissing Bear in bed. Navarrette requested that Barker not tip off Johnston to any of her scene prep so that he’d be genuinely shocked by her (and Nikki’s) decisions.

“I kindly asked Curry if we could not show Michael anything. Even though it doesn’t seem like it, I am quite shy,” she confessed, adding, “Which I think was great because there are so many moments where I scared the shit out of him.”

Barker and Navarrette also discussed some crucial changes that Navarrette made to the character of Nikki, who was originally written “as the girl next door.” According to Navarrette, Barker was “incredibly game for ideas,” including her idea to call Bear “babe” and act “playfully flirty” toward him.

“I wanted the audience to understand why Bear would have the obsession because everything is seen from Bear’s perspective — her laughter, her enticement,” she shared. “I wanted to show what would convince Bear to make that wish.”

At one point during the chat, Kuplowsky brought up the “memeification” of Nikki online, which Navarrette addressed.

“You know, sometimes I feel like it’s not for me, you know what I mean? Because there are so many things growing up that I got to experience of other people,” she offered. “So, I just kind of roll with it. It’s not really for me to analyze one way or the other. It’s kind of for you guys and I love that.”

“It starts to feel like it’s not mine anymore,” Barker said of the life his film has taken online. “It’s not mine anymore.”

Growing up, Navarrette said she was inspired by “Léon: The Professional,” which taught her that young people could act too. She also spoke about how Charlize Theron’s Oscar-winning performance as serial killer Aileen Wuornos in “Monster” made her want to modify her looks for future roles, and, ultimately, how different things are for her since that fateful TIFF premiere.

“Everything changed for me,” she admitted. “I am now in rooms that I could not even imagine. I’m now pitching my own projects and am hopefully able to produce and direct my own stuff. It’s been really, really exciting because I love cinema and I love filmmaking and being a part of Midnight Madness last year lit that fire for me … My whole life has changed, and I just take it day by day.”

title: Watch Brandi Carlile and Bonnie Raitt Duet on ‘Love Me Like a Man’ for ‘Austin City Limits’ Premiere, Plus a Web-Only Bonus, ‘Angel From Montgomery’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: For the season premiere of “Austin City Limits,” Brandi Carlile is officially the one being feted, as the episode finds her formally inducted into the Austin City Limits Hall of Fame. But who’s honoring who is an open question, as the 2026-27 kickoff episode finds Carlile joined by Bonnie Raitt, bringing together two of the […]
content:
For the season premiere of “Austin City Limits,” Brandi Carlile is officially the one being feted, as the episode finds her formally inducted into the Austin City Limits Hall of Fame. But who’s honoring who is an open question, as the 2026-27 kickoff episode finds Carlile joined by Bonnie Raitt, bringing together two of the greatest voices of their respective generations in a mutual admiration society. When the hour-long program airs on PBS stations Saturday night, viewers will get to see their joint performance of Raitt’s classic “Love Me Like a Man” as part of a show that otherwise consists of selections from Carlile’s latest album, “Returning to Myself.” You can get a sneak preview of that with Variety‘s exclusive premiere of the Carlile/Raitt team-up. But there’s more. Recorded during the taping, but not included in the PBS airing, is a second duet, offered here as a web-only only bonus, with the two singers joining forced for John Prine‘s “Angel From Montgomery,” which Raitt brought to its greatest public attention in the 1970s. “We miss John and we’re gonna hold him in our hearts right now,” Raitt says in her introduction. Watch it below.

The episode premieres on most PBS stations Saturday at 8 p.m. CT/9 p.m. ET (check local listings). The full episode is available to stream at PBS.org and on the PBS App. All Season 52 episodes, including Carlile’s Hall of Fame hour, will also be available to stream free on the ACLTV YouTube Channel.

“For more than half a century now ‘Austin City Limits’ has been a loving home to all kinds of real music and the real people that make it,” says Raitt in her introduction of Carlile as an ACL honoree. “There’s really no one quite like her. The most amazing range in voice, clarion and clear and powerful, and as far-reaching as her songs and lyrics.”

Carlile goes on to recall her first journey to Austin with comrades Tim and Phil Hanseroth. “Me and my brothers… first rolled into Austin in our old Chevy van, White Lightning it was called, over 20 years ago,” she says. “I remember getting to town and wanting two things: Tex-Mex and to know where Austin City Limits was taped.” She notes that, thanks to the program, she was more familiar with the Austin skyline than her native Seattle skyline growing up.

Popular on Variety

Brandi Carlile receives her Austin City Limits Hall of Fame honor David Brendan Hall

In the lead-in to “Love Me Like a Man,” Raitt says, “I’m so excited that you picked this song and I was so surprised.” She doesn’t say whether the surprise is because the tune is an “unapologetic blues song,” as Carlile notes, or because Carlile is usually not singing about a man’s loving as the apex of her experience. (She changes the gender in the verse to “a woman who can take me home instead of taking me for a ride,” but leaves the chorus as-is when she’s pairing her voice with Raitt’s.) Carlile tells Raitt that it’s “one of my favorite songs that you’ve ever done,… The guitar playing alone is about the sexiest thing I’ve ever been able to fathom, until you factor in the lyrics from this song… So i sent her a little note, and she rolled her eyes at me, but she said, “Sure, Brandi.”

The part of the PBS program that features Carlile with her band includes one other cover, Alanis Morissette’s “Uninvited,” which she has lately made a regular part of her touring setlist, plus the originals “Returning to Myself,” “No One Knows Us,” “Human,” “Church & State” and “You Without Me.”

Brandi Carlile receives her Austin City Limits Hall of Fame honor David Brendan Hall

Carlile is about to wrap up her “Returning to Myself” U.S. tour in San Diego Sept. 22, but she has an intriguing spinoff album release on the horizon for Sept. 25: a rearranged and re-recorded version of the most recent album that is being dubbed “Returning to Myself… (Sad Gay Version).” The streaming version comes out then and the vinyl is due Dec. 11.

title: ‘It: Welcome to Derry’ Creators Andy and Barbara Muschietti on Late Tim Curry: ‘His Legacy Is Incredible’
summary: More than three decades after Tim Curry originated the role of Pennywise in “It,” his impact is still felt across the franchise and horror fans alike.  “His legacy is incredible, and we’re very thankful that sometimes our name pops up somewhere close to his,” Barbara Muschietti, the co-creator of the “It” prequel series “Welcome to […]
content:
More than three decades after Tim Curry originated the role of Pennywise in “It,” his impact is still felt across the franchise and horror fans alike.

“His legacy is incredible, and we’re very thankful that sometimes our name pops up somewhere close to his,” Barbara Muschietti, the co-creator of the “It” prequel series “Welcome to Derry,” tells Variety. “We will continue watching his incredible movies, and he’ll be in our hearts forever.”

Curry died Aug. 25 from coronary artery disease. He was 80 years old. Although his performance as Pennywise had a profound impact on audiences, Andy Muschietti, Barbara’s brother and co-creator of “Welcome to Derry,” says the actor’s legacy extends far beyond the iconic horror role, pointing to projects including “The Rocky Horror Picture Show,” “Annie” and his musical career.

Popular on Variety

“It’s a shame. It’s bitter, but we’ll remember him,” Andy says. “We’ll cherish it.”

The sibling director-producer duo revamped the world of Pennywise the Dancing Clown in 2017 with a new adaptation of Stephen King’s “It.” Starring Bill Skarsgård as the shapeshifting antagonist, the film was followed by “It Chapter Two” in 2019. The Muschiettis subsequently expanded the franchise with the HBO prequel series, “It: Welcome to Derry.”

Recently renewed for Season 2, the inaugural season of the show premiered on HBO Max on Oct. 26, 2025, and was set in Derry in 1962, detailing the town’s last encounter with Pennywise prior to the 2017 film. Season 2 will jump back to 1935 and, according to the series’ logline, “centers on the bloody massacre of the Bradley Gang, a group of bank robbers who stop in Derry to buy ammo and end up facing unimaginable horror.”

The Bradley Gang Massacre is one of the interludes featured in King’s novel, which Andy teased the second season will incorporate more of. Production hasn’t yet begun, but the director says creatives are currently working on casting.

“It’s a completely different world with a lot of surprises,” Andy says of the sophomore season. “If you like Season 1, you’re going to like Season 2 even more.”

“It: Welcome to Derry” was developed for TV by the Muschiettis and Jason Fuchs, who also worked on the recent “It” films. The siblings previously told Variety they planned to tell the story across three seasons, corresponding with the three cycles of Pennywise in 1962, 1935 and 1908.

The Muschiettis were at the opening night of “It” at the Cosm in Los Angeles, which transforms the film into an immersive, shared-reality experience.

“It feels great,” Andy says about bringing “It” to life in a new way. “I mean, let alone having the opportunity to show the movie again to a big audience, which is a golden opportunity because most filmmakers don’t have the chance. But these guys created something very special.”

“It” at the Cosm is currently available at select locations, but Barbara shares she hopes the experience will eventually expand to cities across the country.

“Anything to bring people to the theaters,” she says, “which is what we make movies for.”

The Cosm’s presentation of “It” runs until Oct. 18. Tickets are available now on the Cosm website.

title: Amy Ryan Joins Emilia Jones In Netflix Drama Series ‘The Retrievals’ From Molly Smith Metzler
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Amy Ryan (Birdman) is set to star opposite Emilia Jones in The Retrievals, Netflix’s third series from Maid and Sirens creator/executive producer Molly Smith Metzler. Inspired by the Peabody-winning NYT podcast by Susan Burton, The Retrievals follows an unlikely community of IVF patients who come together to crusade against Yale University after they are […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Amy Ryan (Birdman) is set to star opposite Emilia Jones in The Retrievals, Netflix‘s third series from Maid and Sirens creator/executive producer Molly Smith Metzler.

Inspired by the Peabody-winning NYT podcast by Susan Burton, The Retrievals follows an unlikely community of IVF patients who come together to crusade against Yale University after they are operated on without anesthesia–because a nurse stole their fentanyl.

Ryan will play Carla Russo, a veteran nurse at Yale Fertility Center who pleads guilty to diverting vast amounts of fentanyl and diluting it with saline, forcing many patients to endure egg retrieval surgery without anesthesia.

Jones plays Gabby Clemente, one of Carla’s victims who leads a groundbreaking legal battle against Yale University.

Watch on Deadline

Metzler is writer and showrunner. She executive produces via her Quiet Coyote banner alongside her Maid and Sirens collaborators Colin McKenna and LuckyChap. Serving as exec producers for LuckyChap are Dani Gorin, Tom Ackerley, and Margot Robbie. Additional executive producers include Caitlin Roper for The New York Times, and podcast write Burton.

Also reuniting with Metzler is Lila Neugebauer, who directed one episode each of Maid and Sirens. She will direct the pilot episode of The Retrievals and executive produce.

Thismarks the first series regular role for Ryan, an Oscar nominee for Gone Baby Gone. In TV, she is known for her major recurring roles on HBO’s The Wire, NBC’s The Office, Hulu’s Only Murders In the Building and, most recently, Season 1 of Apple TV’s Sugar. She will next be seen in Tom McCarthy’s A Statement, which will premiere at the New York Film Festival. Ryan is repped by Gersh and Brecheen Feldman Breimer Silver Thompson.

title: South Korean Monster Thriller ‘Hope’, Andrew Garfield In ‘The Uprising’, Doc ‘Black Zombie’ & Comedy ‘On A String’ – Specialty Preview
summary: South Korean sci-fi thriller Hope joins actioner Runner, historical epic The Uprising and a handful of interesting limited releases this weekend, a few by new indie distributors. With fall festival season in full swing and eyes on the next crop of independent standouts, it’s slower for new entrants in the specialty space. Wide: Neon is […]
content:
South Korean sci-fi thriller Hope joins actioner Runner, historical epic The Uprising and a handful of interesting limited releases this weekend, a few by new indie distributors. With fall festival season in full swing and eyes on the next crop of independent standouts, it’s slower for new entrants in the specialty space.

Wide: Neon is out with Cannes-premiering Hope by Na Hong-jin (The Chaser, The Yellow Sea) at 1,560 theaters. It opened Wednesday, grossing $1.1 million (plus previews of $305k). In the remote South Korea village of Hope Harbor, police chief Bum-seok (Hwang Jung- min) and fellow officer Sung-ae (Hoyeon) are called to find a mysterious creature that has wreaked havoc on the town. In the nearby forest, a coterie of hunters including Sung- ki (Zo In-Sung) set out to track the beast and find themselves hunted instead. The film was a massive hit its home territory of South Korea, where it was released in July, grossing $36 million. See Deadline review.

From Focus Features, The Uprising by Paul Greengrass is new on 2,055 screens. Andrew Garfield toplines as the leader of a ferocious 1381 rebellion against the tyrannical King Richard II. Set against the true events that inspired the legend of Robin Hood, he forms an army of the people in a fight for justice. With Jamie Bell, Stephen Dillane, Tom Hollander, Cosmo Jarvis, Thomasin McKenzie, Jonny Lee Miller, Woody Norman, Katherine Waterston and Sky Yang. Jason Blum produces. See Deadline review.

Watch on Deadline

RELATED: How Paul Greengrass And Andrew Garfield Made ‘The Uprising’s 14th-Century History Into A Modern-Day Truth

Angel Studios debuts Australia-set action thriller Runner by Scott Waughon on 2,581 screens. Alan Ritchson (Reacher) moves to the big screen as a former soldier and war hero-turned-courier is thrown into a brutal race against time when a critical medical delivery makes him and his unlikely partner (Owen Wilson) the targets of a ruthless cartel. As the mission spirals into a deadly manhunt, they must survive the chase and deliver their cargo to save the life of a little girl. Written by Miles Hubley and Tommy White.

Limited: If I Go Will They Miss Me, written and directed by Walter Thompson-Hernandez opens at L.A.’s AMC Century City for a special engagement, expanding to about 30 markets next week. Distributed by Rich Spirit, which acquired it out of Sundance. Stars Danielle Brooks (also an EP), J. Alphonse Nicholson and newcomer Bodhi Dell. Set in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles, the pic based on Thompson-Hernandez’s Sundance 2022 short film revolves around 12-year-old Lil Ant (Dell), who struggles to connect with a distant father. Grammy and Oscar winner Jon Batiste is an EP and recorded a cover of Dinah Washington’s song “This Bitter Earth” for the film. A strong festival runs includes Best Narrative Award at the Bentonville Film Festival.

Musician-turned-comedian Isabel Hagen’s feature directorial debut On A String, the first release from Joke Zero, opens at the Quad Cinema in New York with five more markets set for next week. Winner of Best Screenplay in a U.S. Narrative Feature at the 2025 Tribeca Festival, it’s the first foray into distribution for Joke Zero, filmmaker Brandon Tamburri’s comedy-focused production company. The pic is inspired by Hagen’s real-life experiences, and she stars as a Juilliard-trained violinist navigating the New York City freelance classical musician scene while living with her oddball family. With Dylan Baker, Eric Bogosian, Frederick Weller and Jamie Lee.

Kino Lorber’s SXSW-premiering documentary Black Zombie by Canadian director Maya Annik Bedward opens in New York (Quad) and LA (Nuart). Bedward is in NYC for opening weekend Q&As. Her feature directorial debut traces the evolution of the zombie from colonial Haiti to contemporary Hollywood, digging beneath the blood-soaked spectacle of modern horror to uncover the creature’s buried and unsettling origins. Long before it became associated with flesh-eating ghouls, the zombie was a living metaphor for slavery — not a monster, but the ultimate victim of colonial power. Featuring interviews with Yves-Grégory Francois, Slash, Tom Savini, Anderson Mojica, Erol Josué, Mambo Labelle Deese Bonica, Tananarive Due and Zandashé Brown. Took the Northern Excellence Award for the standout Canadian film at Fantasia International Film Festival.

Outsider Pictures debuts TIFF 2025 Centerpiece film The Condor Daughter (La Hija Cóndor) at Cinema Village in NYC this week, Laemmle L.A. next. Written and directed by Alvaro Olmos Torrico, Bolivia’s International Oscar entry is the story of Clara (Marisol Vallejo Montañor), a teenager growing up in a small indigenous community high in the Andes. Her adoptive mother Ana (María Magdalena Sanizo), a midwife, has taught her the ancient songs used to guide women through childbirth, melodies passed down for generations, but Clara dreams of becoming a folk music star in the big city. Awarded Best Film at Biarritz Latin American Film Festival. Montañor took Best Actress at the Malaga and Guadalajara fests.

Mighty Mary documentary from filmmaker and Olympic rower Mary Mazzio (I Am Jane Doe, A Hero for Daisy) in partnership with Skydance Sports opens for a weeklong run at about a dozen AMC theaters, including the AMC Empire in NYC and AMC Town Center in L.A.. Mazzio’s production company 50 Eggs Films handled distribution. The doc narrated by Elizabeth Banks and Hugh Jackman (also EPs) follows the first-ever all-women’s sailing crew to vie for the famed America’s Cup in 1995. The doc premiered at the Nantucket Film Festival in June, with many of the sailors from the Mighty Mary in attendance. Widely dismissed at the time as a publicity stunt, the women — a group of world-class and Olympic sailors, rowers and trailblazing women athletes from across the country — defied expectations to become legitimate contenders in one of the most demanding competitions in sports. See Deadline interview with Mazzio.

title: A24 Boards SCP Foundation Movie From Spooky Pictures & Image Nation, Sets 2027 Release
summary: EXCLUSIVE: A24 is teaming with Spooky Pictures and Image Nation Studios to bring the SCP Foundation, one of the internet’s largest fan-built horror and science-fiction universes, to the big screen for the first time. Taking worldwide rights to the project, an untitled extension of the V/H/S horror series, A24 is targeting a 2027 theatrical release. Plot details are […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: A24 is teaming with Spooky Pictures and Image Nation Studios to bring the SCP Foundation, one of the internet’s largest fan-built horror and science-fiction universes, to the big screen for the first time.

Taking worldwide rights to the project, an untitled extension of the V/H/S horror series, A24 is targeting a 2027 theatrical release.

Plot details are being kept under wraps. A24 will co-produce with Roy Lee and Steven Schneider for Spooky Pictures, alongside Josh Goldbloom, who has worked on past V/H/S entries including V/H/S/94, V/H/S/99 and V/H/S/Halloween, and Michael Schreiber, who also worked across multiple installments.

Image Nation Studios’ CEO Ben Ross and Spooky Pictures’ Rami Yasin and Jakob Pollack will exec produce alongside Brad Miska.

Watch on Deadline

Originating online in 2008, the SCP Foundation has since evolved into a sprawling, collaborative mythology created and expanded by thousands of contributors around the world. Encompassing a library of anomalous objects, entities, phenomena and stories, this universe has a lore all its own, involving a secret organization covertly operating to protect humanity from malevolent entities.

A24 comes to the feature take following its success with Backrooms, the horror film from Kane Parsons, which grossed over $394M worldwide. Like that universe, the SCP Foundation emerged from a creepypasta, or short, user-generated horror story/urban legend, posted to the 4chan internet forum. Prior to this new film, fandom around SCP Foundation spurred the creation of assorted games, short films, and web series.

Speaking to the impetus for the SCP Foundation movie, Image Nation Studios’ Ross and Spooky Pictures co-founders Lee and Schneider said: “Internet lore is quickly rising as a compelling source of new stories for the horror genre, bringing with it built-in, highly devoted audiences. As fans increasingly seek out fresh scares, we’re focused on tapping into the most compelling online worlds in which talent already live, such as the vast SCP universe, and helping them make the leap to the big screen. With A24’s expertise in nurturing and elevating internet-born phenomena like Backrooms into major theatrical success, they’re the ideal partner for V/H/S: SCP and we can’t wait to expand the franchise with new, spine chilling stories together.”

Image Nation Studios and Spooky Pictures announced their acquisition of rights to the V/H/S found-footage horror anthology franchise earlier this year. V/H/S: SCP marks the next installment in the series, following V/H/S/Mixtape, a music-themed anthology premiering on Shudder this October.

Alongside Blumhouse Atomic Monster and Divide/Conquer, Spooky Pictures is also one of the companies behind Josh Giuliano’s new horror film Occupant for Focus Features that we just announced.

title: Gary Oldman Reveals Jack Lowden’s Response To His Bond Comments
summary: “It’s Deadline Hollywood, so I’m going to set the record straight,” Gary Oldman said during an interview on Friday at Deadline’s Toronto Film Festival studio. He was, of course, referring to the recent furor around some off-the-cuff remarks he made about the casting of James Bond in a recent interview, and the resulting speculation that […]
content:
“It’s Deadline Hollywood, so I’m going to set the record straight,” Gary Oldman said during an interview on Friday at Deadline’s Toronto Film Festival studio.

He was, of course, referring to the recent furor around some off-the-cuff remarks he made about the casting of James Bond in a recent interview, and the resulting speculation that Oldman’s Slow Horses co-star Jack Lowden might be the new 007 in the upcoming Denis Villeneuve-directed Bond film.

Oldman told Deadline his words had been entirely misconstrued and spun into suggestive headlines by the media. And that he’d relayed that fact to Lowden on the phone.

Watch on Deadline

Oldman smiled as he recalled the conversation. “What did Jack say? He said ‘Oh, they do that kind of thing, the f*ckers.'”

Here’s the official setting straight of the record from Oldman: “A Canadian journalist [from the outlet Global] asked me about Jack Lowden and the James Bond connection. I did not bring this up. I did not offer this up. She said, ‘So how do you feel about it?’ So I said, ‘Well, they got the six guys because they published the picture of the contenders for the role.’ I said, ‘Rumor has it that they picked someone, but they’ve not announced it yet. And fingers crossed for Jack.’ And they made it sound like I had a hotline to Denis [Villeneuve]! And he was feeding me the information. So they took it to the very edge of misquoting me, moved things around like they do, and it became a headline.”

RELATED: The Obsession For The Next ‘Obsession’ At TIFF: Festival Hot List Includes Pics For Sale With Cynthia Erivo, Chase Infiniti, The Maras, Dave Bautista & More

Oldman was in Toronto with some of the Slow Horses team (sans Lowden) as part of TIFF’s Primetime lineup, which spotlights television. With him at the Deadline studio were Saskia Reeves, Christopher Chung, Aimee-Ffion Edwards, Ruth Bradley and director Adam Randall.

“We’re rooting for him, aren’t we?” Oldman said of Lowden. Looking around the room at the Slow Horses team, he received vigorous nods all round.

Slow Horses Season 6 drops September 16 on Apple TV, with production already ramping up for Season 7. In Season 6, which is based on the sixth and seventh books of Mick Herron’s Slough House series titled Joe Country and Slough House, we’ll see Oldman’s character Jackson Lamb galvanized into action when he realizes the Slow Horses are being systematically targeted and Lowden’s character River will face the return of not one, but two significant figures from the past.

RELATED: 2026 Premiere Dates For New & Returning Series On Broadcast, Streaming & Cable

As for Bond, the ultimate casting mystery remains unsolved. Alongside Lowden, the list of rumored contenders includes Callum Turner, Dev Patel, Paul Mescal, Jacob Elordi, Harris Dickinson and Jack Barton.

title: ‘The Uprising’ Star Woody Norman on the ‘Power Trip’ Playing King Richard II and Going Meatless at Age 10 After Working With Joaquin Phoenix
summary: Filming “The Uprising” gave British actor Woody Norman, who plays 14-year-old King Richard II in the historical fiction drama, a massive headache. It turns out the only crown they had for him to use during the shoot got damaged the first day of filming. “So it didn’t fit my head,” Norman, 17, tells me over […]
content:
Filming “The Uprising” gave British actor Woody Norman, who plays 14-year-old King Richard II in the historical fiction drama, a massive headache.

It turns out the only crown they had for him to use during the shoot got damaged the first day of filming. “So it didn’t fit my head,” Norman, 17, tells me over Zoom from a hotel room in Los Angeles just a few hours before the movie’s premiere at the DGA in West Hollywood. “I would leave every day with a splitting headache because it was bent. We had put foam in it, but it didn’t work. It was steel against my head.”

“The Uprising,” written and directed by Paul Greengrass, is based on the real-life Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 England. Andrew Garfield toplines the film as a fictional farmer – known only as Ploughman – who sparks and helps lead thousands of commoners on a march to protest the king in London.

Popular on Variety

In addition to the dented crown, Norman had to endure the royal wardrobe, including “really heavy” robes. “I don’t weigh much,” he tells me later on the red carpet at the premiere. “I weigh 46 kilograms [about 101 pounds] and they weigh as much as I do, so it was really really painful.”

Even so, it’s fun to be king. “It’s a power trip,” Norman says. “All of the supporting actors would go, ‘Your highness,’ and they would bow to me when I walked by. That really got to my head because they would do it every day.”

Tom Hollander as Treasurer Hales, Woody Norman as King RIchard II and Katherine Waterston as The Countess in “The Uprising.”

Betina La Plante/Focus Features. © 2026 All Rights Reserved.

Norman’s first day shooting with Garfield was a pivotal fight scene between Ploughman and the king. “I was very intimidated,” Norman says. “It’s Andrew Garfield, you know that’s big. He immediately went, ‘I love you, and come on, come on!’ I was like, ‘OK,, we’re both actors. We can do this.’ It completely removed that sense of awe and made us both professionals. We’re here to do a job. Let’s do it together. I’m very, very grateful for that.”

The scene involved Ploughman shoving a paper scroll into the king’s mouth. “I have an Invisalign wire in my teeth,” Norman says. “The paper was in my teeth until after we wrapped. It was cool to rub my tongue on my on my teeth and go, ‘Oh, the uprising.’”

Norman first gained attention when he was just 10 years old and starred opposite Joaquin Phoenix in the 2021 Mike Mills drama “C’mon C’mon.” “One of the great men on the planet is Joaquin,” Norman says. “I don’t know if I would still be acting if I didn’t work with him.”

He continues, “I didn’t really understand what I was. I didn’t know I was an actor. I didn’t know this was a job. I was having fun, and then he made me realize that it doesn’t have to be a job. It’s a way of living. It’s a way of creating, and you know, now after working with Joaquin, I’m fully vegan because of course I am.”

Norman laughs.

“There was a interaction we had where I was eating meat and he was like, ‘Why don’t you just stop eating meat?’” he remembers. “And then I said, ‘Why don’t you stop smoking?’ He’s still smoking, so he hasn’t kept up his bit.”

Up next? Variety’s Leo Barraclough exclusively reported that Norman will star in the British urban horror thriller “Skag & Bone” along with Malachi Kirby, Tuppence Middleton, Conrad Khan, Kola Bokinni.

“The Uprising” is in theaters now.

title: Ocean Way Festival Featuring Killers, Olivia Dean and Jack White Is Canceled, as Santa Monica Blames Beach Damage From Hurricane Forces
summary: Ocean Way is going away, at least for a year. Goldenvoice’s inaugural Ocean Way Festival, which was scheduled to take place on the beach in Santa Monica Sept. 26-27, has been called off, with city officials saying the culprit is erosion along the shore caused by recent hurricane-level forces off the coast. A statement from […]
content:
Ocean Way is going away, at least for a year. Goldenvoice‘s inaugural Ocean Way Festival, which was scheduled to take place on the beach in Santa Monica Sept. 26-27, has been called off, with city officials saying the culprit is erosion along the shore caused by recent hurricane-level forces off the coast.

A statement from the city of Santa Monica said that the festival “has been canceled after storm surf generated by Hurricane Marie and runoff from a storm drain outfall eroded a large portion of the festival site over Labor Day weekend. The beach can no longer safely accommodate the festival production and audience capacity, and with construction and load-in set to begin next week, the city determined that cancellation was the only responsible option. Plans are already underway to bring the Ocean Way Festival back to Santa Monica in 2027.”

The statement further explained that “the surf stripped sand from the beach south of the Pier, which would have required moving the safe shoreline setback for the festival 96 feet inland. At the same time, runoff from the Pico-Kenter Storm Drain outfall cut through the southern end of the site, forcing the festival’s southern boundary to move around 500 hundred feet to the north… City staff completed an assessment of the site, evaluating sand conditions, emergency vehicle access, construction & load-in requirements, crowd circulation, tides, and the extended forecast. The combined loss of usable beach meant the festival infrastructure could not be built and the event would not be safe for attendees on the smaller footprint that remained.

Popular on Variety

The statement sent to ticketholders further said that refunds for passes, which had been sold in a range from $249 to $2,250, will be processed automatically in the next 5-7 business days.

The two-day festival was hoping to draw up to 45,000 to the beach each day. Single-day passes were being sold along with two-day entry, and the lineup seemed designed to possibly draw a somewhat different audience each day, with rock acts like the Killers, Jack White and Sublime topping the bill on Saturday and a more eclectic lineup headed by Olivia Dean, Khruangbin and Durand Jones & the Indications on Sunday.

First-time beach-based festivals seem to be having a hard time of it in SoCal this year, with the inaugural LA Jazz Festival — which had a key stage set for Dockweiler Beach — having been canceled at the last minute, although the reasons given for that one had to do with finances and prep. At least anyone who wants to hear music with an ocean breeze still has an option for Eddie Vedder’s annual Ohana Fest. It takes place alongside the beach in Orange County’s Dana Point Sept. 25-27 — and, obviously, it no longer has Ocean Way as competition the same weekend.

“We’ve spent more than a year on this festival, and I’ve spent most of it telling anyone who would listen that music was coming back to this beach,” said Santa Monica mayor Caroline Torosis, in a statement. “I wanted to stand on the sand, see the Pier lit up behind that stage, and sing along with our community. I feel for the fans, the artists, and the businesses counting on that weekend, and I’m right there with them. But the surf took the beach we planned this on, and we cannot put tens of thousands of festival-goers on that sand until it’s safe,” “What didn’t wash away is the partnership. Goldenvoice has been a responsible partner from day one, and that work continues. Next year, the show goes on.”

“While we share everyone’s disappointment that the show can’t go on this year, we fully support the city’s decision to prioritize safety, and we believe canceling for 2026 is the right call,” said Goldenvoice Chief Operating Officer Melissa Ormond. “We are committed to returning to Santa Monica in 2027 and delivering the Ocean Way Festival experience we envisioned for the community, artists and fans.”

Variety published an interview in July with Goldenvoice producer Nic Adler, son of the legendary Lou Adler, about the desire to bring music back in a big way to Santa Monica, which has hosted few big rock or pop shows since the historic Santa Monica Civic Auditorium fell into disuse.

Said Adler then, “Really where it stems from is that Santa Monica is kind of having its own revitalization moment or realignment plan, turning toward events, culture, arts and music to get people to come to the city. Santa Monica is an interesting place because it’s almost like an underdog city a little bit, in our backyard. We all know Santa Monica’s there, but I think they want to make sure that those memories stick.”

He noted, “This was a little bit like, ‘OK, we’re in Santa Monica, we’re on the beach, the sun’s setting — of course I wanna hear Khruangbin.’ The lineup took some inspiration from the location, and I’d probably say that’s not an everyday for Goldenvoice.”

title: Pink Explains Slamming Macklemore’s Pro-Palestine Performances, Acknowledges Heavy Backlash: ‘I’m Standing Up for My Own People, and I Thought I Knew How Lonely That Would Be. It’s Lonelier Than That’
summary: Pink had fallen silent in the face of backlash from many quarters following her reposting a call for Macklemore to be dropped from the Ed Sheeran tour in the wake of his nightly pro-Palestinian songs and statements. Now she has spoken up about the controversy and her part in it in a big way, with […]
content:
Pink had fallen silent in the face of backlash from many quarters following her reposting a call for Macklemore to be dropped from the Ed Sheeran tour in the wake of his nightly pro-Palestinian songs and statements. Now she has spoken up about the controversy and her part in it in a big way, with a 1,300-word social media post that has her exploring why she repeated the sentiments asking Sheeran to drop Macklemore, why his statements alarmed her as a Jewish woman, and how it has felt “lonely” facing an onslaught of criticism this week.

The singer noted that she may have been a typical “cheap and fast” social media user when she first reposted the anti-Macklemore meme, rather than speaking up in her own words, which she is now belatedly doing. “A repost isn’t a statement, and a meme isn’t a spine,” she argued, saying that she would “rather be disagreed with for what I actually said than hated for what anybody else wrote, so let me say it.”

Popular on Variety

Pink noted how her feelings about Macklemore have evolved, from support for him when “I was in the room at the Grammys in 2014 when Macklemore rapped ‘Same Love’ and 33 couples, gay and straight, got married to it, and I cheered, no questions asked.” Then, she pointed out an antisemitic costume the rapper wore a short time later, for which he subsequently issued a mea culpa. “Macklemore put on a hooked nose, a black beard and a bowl cut, performed in it, and called it a ‘random costume.’ Every Jew I know knew exactly what it was. The same love, it turned out, had a guest list, and we weren’t on it. But he apologized, and I let it go, because that’s what we do. We let it go.” Nonetheless, she suggested, his wearing of the costume informed how his statements might be received in years to come.

The singer said that “last weekend he stood in front of a stadium full of music-loving families, with violent images from a war on the screens, dedicated a song to the movement of his choice, and then took the mic to tell all of the Jews in the stadium that it wasn’t about them.” She added: “You don’t get to decide that for us.”

Her current position, as she explained it in her post: “Of course I don’t speak for Israel, or for any government. I never have. What I said in October 2023 is still exactly what I believe: Hamas is a terrorist organization. Palestinians deserve a future that honors their humanity and their aspirations. Protecting innocent life comes first, everywhere, and nobody should ever celebrate the death of a child. Anybody’s child. I’ve spent a decade as a UNICEF ambassador for kids who didn’t choose the country or the war they were born into, and I have grieved every one of them, on both sides of that fence. I didn’t do it from behind a screen; I went to those children and held them. I’m not going to litigate a complex war in an Instagram caption, and I’m not going to recite anybody’s slogan to earn back a follower.”

The singer declared that her response earlier this week was prompted not by Macklemore saying “Free Palestine,” but by his statements on stage — in response to the backlash he was facing from some quarters — that his statements were aimed at Israel, not all Jews.

“That’s what prompted my repost. Not ‘Free Palestine,’ and not anyone’s right to say it. I have never asked for another artist to be silenced and I’m not asking now. I don’t need anyone fired, and I don’t need a refund. What I need is to be able to say, as a Jewish mom, ‘that scared me, and it scared people I love,”’without being told our fear is just propaganda, and without being told I’m somehow cool with genocide because I noticed?”

Pink pointed to some of the causes she has supported over the years that have drawn fire, mostly from the right wing. “I have stood up for other people’s people my whole career, and I know exactly what it costs. And now I’m standing up for my own people, and I thought I knew going in how lonely that would be. And it’s lonelier than that. But I’m doing it anyway.”



She added, “Something has changed in this country, and I can read it in my own comments. ‘From the river to the sea.’ ‘Zionist,’ spat like it’s a slur, by people who couldn’t tell you the details of what I believe, because I hadn’t told them yet. I wasn’t asked. I was told. I don’t think most of them hate Jews. I think somebody handed them a story where the Jew who won’t apologize for existing must be the villain, and they’ve been putting words in my mouth ever since.”

On her Instagram post, Pink divided her lengthy statement into two parts, the first half of it coming in the post itself and the second in the comments. But the second half is no longer visible. An hour or so after posting, as pro and con responses accumulated from fans and detractors, she opted to switch off commenting for that post. Unfortunately for her ability to explain herself, cutting off comments meant she also eliminated her own comment that contained the crux of her explanation. But you can read it all below, including the part she inadvertently deleted.

Before Pink or her social administrator cut off comments on her post, the responses were sharply divided, with mostly hostile or disappointed comments appearing at the top of the replies, followed by many supportive ones echoing her “Shana tova” sign-off further down. Among the negative replies, before all were blocked: “A repost is a statement. Just saying. (esp w 11M followers).” “Said all this to say nothing at all. This was truly not on my bingo card. Doubling down is insane as well.” “I grew up respecting your rebellion against things that were wrong in the world. But now you seem to have switched to supporting those very same people that cause the pain to children and women. I hope that is how you want to be remembered.”

And a sampling of the positive replies: “This was beautiful. And not trite. And not prepared by AI or a publicist. This was an authentic monologue and I appreciate so much how strong you are. And I’m proud to have you in my same tribe.” “I wish all other Jewish celebrities were as brave as you. We love you.”

In his most recent comments addressing the controversy, Macklemore said, “To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace; love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality…. So I say free Palestine, I say free Lebanon, I say free Cuba, I say free Congo, free Sudan, I say free all people in America living in fear of this terrorist organization, ICE. None of us will be free until we are all free.”

Pink’s statement, in full:

I’ve been quiet in my own words for a week, which you know isn’t like me. So here they are.



Last Sunday I reposted somebody else’s post about Macklemore’s set at Ed Sheeran’s show. It said things in words I didn’t write, and I wouldn’t have chosen all of them. Then the comments came, and I did what I do when I’m hurt, which is post snarky memes and act like I’m fine. That’s on me. A repost isn’t a statement, and a meme isn’t a spine. Social media makes all of us cheap and fast, and we all know it. But I’d rather be disagreed with for what I actually said than hated for what anybody else wrote, so let me say it.



I was born a Jew. I didn’t pick it, and I’ve never hidden it. And this week a whole lot of people decided what I believe without asking me, without checking a single thing I’ve ever said or done, because a repost and the word “Jew” were apparently enough to fill in the rest. But let me fill it in… myself.



Of course I don’t speak for Israel, or for any government. I never have. What I said in October 2023 is still exactly what I believe: Hamas is a terrorist organization. Palestinians deserve a future that honors their humanity and their aspirations. Protecting innocent life comes first, everywhere, and nobody should ever celebrate the death of a child. Anybody’s child. I’ve spent a decade as a UNICEF ambassador for kids who didn’t choose the country or the war they were born into, and I have grieved every one of them, on both sides of that fence. I didn’t do it from behind a screen; I went to those children and held them. I’m not going to litigate a complex war in an Instagram caption, and I’m not going to recite anybody’s slogan to earn back a follower.



Here’s what I was reacting to. I was in the room at the Grammys in 2014 when Macklemore rapped “Same Love” and thirty-three couples, gay and straight, got married to it, and I cheered, no questions asked. Four months later Macklemore put on a hooked nose, a black beard and a bowl cut, performed in it, and called it a “random costume.” Every Jew I know knew exactly what it was. The same love, it turned out, had a guest list, and we weren’t on it. But he apologized, and I let it go, because that’s what we do. We let it go. Then last weekend he stood in front of a stadium full of music-loving families, with violent images from a war on the screens, dedicated a song to the movement of his choice, and then took the mic to tell all of the Jews in the stadium that it wasn’t about them.

You don’t get to decide that for us.

That’s what prompted my repost. Not “Free Palestine,” and not anyone’s right to say it. I have never asked for another artist to be silenced and I’m not asking now. I don’t need anyone fired, and I don’t need a refund. What I need is to be able to say, as a Jewish mom, “that scared me, and it scared people I love,” without being told our fear is just propaganda, and without being told I’m somehow cool with genocide because I noticed?

And please don’t talk to me like I’ve never stood up for my beliefs when it was unpopular. In the middle of the Gulf War in 2006 I put out a song called “Dear Mr. President” and sang it every night on tour while my country was in a war I didn’t support, and I took the hate for it, and I sang it anyway because my sharp criticism was of a government, not this flawed country I love and who my dad fought for. I stood with gay kids before it was fashionable and with trans kids now, when it isn’t, and with their families, and I handed out the books that got banned, and you know I got called every name there is, and I’d do all of it again tomorrow. I have stood up for other people’s people my whole career, and I know exactly what it costs.

And now I’m standing up for my own people, and I thought I knew going in how lonely that would be. And it’s lonelier than that. But I’m doing it anyway.



Something has changed in this country, and I can read it in my own comments. “From the river to the sea.” “Zionist,” spat like it’s a slur, by people who couldn’t tell you the details of what I believe, because I hadn’t told them yet. I wasn’t asked. I was told. I don’t think most of them hate Jews. I think somebody handed them a story where the Jew who won’t apologize for existing must be the villain, and they’ve been putting words in my mouth ever since.



But I’ve been portrayed as the villain before. I can take it. I just won’t take it quietly, and I’m not going to teach my kids to.



So, to the ones who are furious with me: you don’t have to agree with me. You never did. That’s been our unspoken agreement for twenty-five years, and it still stands, and so do I. You don’t have to agree with one thing Israel’s government does to not want the Jewish family two rows down from you to be scared or targeted at a concert. That’s the only thing I’m asking anybody for. To the ones who are frightened this week, Jewish or Muslim or Palestinian or Israeli or just tired of all of it: I see you. And if anybody wants to really know what I think, just ask me. I’m right here. I’ve never been hard to find. And I’ll keep speaking out, in my own words.



It’s Friday. For working people who have more to worry about than pop stars and pile-ons, it’s the end of a hard week. It’s also the 25th anniversary of September 11th, and my prayers are with the innocent souls we lost that morning. And at sundown, for Jews, it’s Rosh Hashanah, our New Year.



Now I’m going to go make dinner for my kids, light the candles, dip some apples in honey, pour a glass of wine and be full of gratitude. That’s my tradition. It also happens to be a Jewish one.



Shana tova.

title: ‘Girl Group’ Review: Rebel Wilson’s Musical Comedy Is Fun Spiritual Sequel To ‘Pitch Perfect’ — Toronto Film Festival
summary: Nearly 15 years after first stealing audiences’ funny bones as Fat Amy, Rebel Wilson has provided a new generation with a musical comedy that will have fans laughing and singing along just the same. In Girl Group, co-written and directed by Wilson, the Australian multihyphenate stars as popstar Tassie Young, who found fame with her […]
content:
Nearly 15 years after first stealing audiences’ funny bones as Fat Amy, Rebel Wilson has provided a new generation with a musical comedy that will have fans laughing and singing along just the same.

In Girl Group, co-written and directed by Wilson, the Australian multihyphenate stars as popstar Tassie Young, who found fame with her four best friends when they were discovered at a talent show in 1996.

But with Tassie’s party girl ways forcing her out of the group in 2006, she finds out her former bandmates are having a reunion tour in the present and don’t want her back.

After a DUI arrest, Tassie is forced to teach music to a group of teen girls at East Hollywood Community Center, where she discovers their talent and helps them prepare for an audition with a major label.

Watch on Deadline

Wilson hits all the right comedic notes as both star and director, complemented by hilarious performances from an ensemble that includes Jennifer Coolidge as her manager, Randall Park as the community center’s director and Derry Girls alum Jamie-Lee O’Donnell as a rival coach with her own girl group.

The movie is also stacked with cameos from the likes of the Spice Girls’ Mel C, Pussycat Dolls’ Nicole Scherzinger, Sally Hawkins, Chris Colfer and more.

With fun choreographed covers of Spice Girls, Destiny’s Child, Billie Eilish, Chappell Roan and others, the ensemble of newcomers puts their talent on full display, in addition to keeping up with their seasoned co-stars’ comedic chops.

Girl Group is an addictively enjoyable film blends heart and humor, and Wilson has returned to her roots with a fun, character-driven musical comedy that is sure to appeal to anyone who couldn’t stop singing “Cups (When I’m Gone)” for the majority of 2011.

Title: Girl Group

Festival: Toronto (Gala Presentations)

Director-screenwriter: Rebel Wilson

Cast: Rebel Wilson, Randall Park, Sheridan Smith, Melanie Chisholm, Nicole Scherzinger, Jamie-Lee O’Donnell, Shaznay Lewis, Ashley Roberts, Judi Love, Guz Khan, Chabely Ponce, Daniela Couso, Lilah Pate, Mia Kaplan, Bailey Stender, Loren Gray, Miracle Washington, Ana Yi Puig, Keith Duffy, Chris Colfer, Bechill, Jolene, Sally Hawkins, Jennifer Coolidge

Sales agents: UTA/Live Nation Studios

Running time: 1 hr 43 mins

title: Russell Crowe Charms 1,400-Strong Venice Audience With ‘What Love Builds’ Doc Charting His Musical Career
summary: Russell Crowe enjoyed an enthusiastic response to his bio-doc meets concert film What Love Builds as it premiered Out of Competition to a 1,400-strong crowd at the Venice Film Festival on Friday evening. The documentary sets out to show that music has been part of Crowes’s life long before he decided to move to Sydney […]
content:
Russell Crowe enjoyed an enthusiastic response to his bio-doc meets concert film What Love Builds as it premiered Out of Competition to a 1,400-strong crowd at the Venice Film Festival on Friday evening.

The documentary sets out to show that music has been part of Crowes’s life long before he decided to move to Sydney from New Zealand in the late 1980s to pursue an acting career, busking on the streets initially to make ends meet.



It features footage showing Crowe’s early musical endeavours from his teen years performing at an Auckland music hall under the stage name of Russ Le Roq, to his 415 performances as Eddie/Dr Scott in a New Zealand production of The Rocky Horror Show.

Crowe also delves into the creation of his first major band 30 Odd Foot of Grunts; its prophetic The Photograph Kills EP, and his abrupt decision to disband it as his acting career took off and he felt his fame was muddying the waters. He suggested a pushy offer from then Sony head Tommy Mottola to sign the band had been the final straw.

Watch on Deadline

In an example of how his love of music has fed into his acting, Crowe reveals how a line in Gladiator in which his character Maximus tells Emperor Marcus Aurelius he has been away for “2 years, 264 days, and this morning” was rewritten at his request and taken inspiration from the line “It’s been seven hours and 15 days” in Prince’s track Nothing Compares 2 U

Later, he recounts how on Ridley Scott’s 2010 Robin Hood, he had been able to influence the casting of the merry men to bring actors who were also musicians. These would include Scott Grimes who would go on to become an occasional member of his current band Indoor Garden Party alongside the likes of Samantha Barks and Alan Doyle.

Crowe also digs into lows of his career such as his arrest in New York in 2005 for assault for throwing a telephone at a hotel employee; “the pain” of being pursued by paparazzi, who he says he is also grateful to for capturing some of his best pictures of him with his children, or the ridiculing of his work as a musician and songwriter.

Footage from the band’s performances intercut throughout film had the Venice audience clapping as if in a concert, with a cover version by Crowe of Dire Straits’ Romeo and Juliet causing the Sala Darsena theater to erupt into full-scale applause.

Russell Crowe breaks into huge smile as 1,400-strong crowd claps to the beat of closing credits of bio-doc come concert film ‘What Love Builds’ at Venice Film Festival pic.twitter.com/zEO5ho8WNa — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 11, 2026

As the credits rolled at the end, spectators clapped to the beat of the final track while a visibly happy Crowe laughed and smiled at the reaction.

Crowe, who wrote, directed and produced the documentary, told a press conference earlier, that the work, showing the central role music has played in his creative life since he was a child, had been 15 years in the making.

“I thought it might take me a year, but as I was doing it, things would come up that I was going to be doing shortly with the music, so I kept waiting for that, and the next thing, and the next thing. By the time we sat down to cut it we had an extensive 18 feet of film,” he said.

“It was massive undertaking to try to chip away at the narrative, but I knew what my intention was, and my intention was to answer the question I get asked probably most and that is to define the difference between music and acting. The film attempts to explain the two things are completely intertwined for me,” he said.

Crowe told the press conference that Venice had been his target festival for the documentary and that he had contacted Italian director Gabriele Muccino, who directed him in Fathers & Daughters, to help connect him with festival director Alberto Barbera.

“As we’re coming towards the end of the cut, I said out loud, the most amazing thing would be if I could get to screen this in Venice. I’ve been to a lot of film festivals, but the most fun film festival is Venice, and there’s depth in the appreciation of the audience,” he said.

“I couldn’t have had a better result as a filmmaker. This thing was just extremely personal, and this is the absolute perfect place,”

title: International Insider: European TV In Peril; Venice & TIFF Latest; Mercedes Ron Interview
summary: Welcome once again, Insiders. Jesse Whittock here to take you through the top film and TV stories from the international community, and you can sign up to the newsletter here. We’re also taking a moment to pay our respects to the victims of 9/11, 25 years ago in New York. European TV In Peril Uneasy […]
content:
Welcome once again, Insiders. Jesse Whittock here to take you through the top film and TV stories from the international community, and you can sign up to the newsletter here. We’re also taking a moment to pay our respects to the victims of 9/11, 25 years ago in New York.

European TV In Peril

Channel 4 series ‘A Woman of Substance’ Banijay Rights/The Forge/Channel 4

Uneasy reading: It was a week of bad numbers for European television, and stats don’t usually lie. They were so bad in France, in fact, that the country’s cultural body the CNC is hastily putting together a symposium to discuss exactly how bleak it all looks. Stewart reported annual French TV exports figures that showed Gallic content sales collapsed to a ten-year low. TV ad revenue declines mean less money for programs, and by extension, less TV to sell abroad. Added to that, while streamer investment in other countries is at least partially offsetting that problem, it’s not happening in France. Here are some of those numbers: International sales for 2025 are down 21.6% year-on-year at €164.2M ($191M) and co-production investment is down 18.7% at €87.7M. Pre-sale revenues also fell apart. Sacre bleu. Over in the UK, the numbers weren’t much better. The annual Pact census revealed the country’s production sector revenues actually hit their second-highest total ever at £3.8B ($5.2B) – suggesting a sector in rude health. However, peering under the bonnet revealed a different picture. The spend from the UK’s broadcasters fell to pre-Covid levels of under £2B and it was international revenue and non-TV assets that pulled the number up. While that shows British content is doing well, and that the country’s production community is becoming more entrepreneurial, it highlights an increasing reliance on global streamers, and Pact CEO Nigel Warner said the fall in network spend – down for a third year in a row – was heaping pressure on smaller and mid-sized independent producers. In a bad week for the UK, Pact said the BBC could be sleepwalking towards “managed decline,” and Channel 4 confirmed the biggest job cuts in its history. Get your umbrellas out, it’s about to start raining. Better news from the cinema sector, where the International Union of Cinemas reported encouraging box office figures from across Europe, the Middle East and Africa. France and Italy both posted record-breaking summer stats, and there were similar sorts of numbers coming from Spain, the Netherlands and the UK, whose picture house body, the UK Cinema Association, released stats showing more than 17 million admissions last month.

Latest From Venice & TIFF

Clockwise from top left: ‘Primetime,’ ‘Ink,’ ‘Bunker,’ ‘The Echo Chamber’ and ‘Bucking Fastard’ A24; Anthony Dickenson; Blue Morning Pictures; Indigo Film; Lena Herzog

Sensational sights and sounds: It’s been an eventful second week in Venice. The films have been strong, and so has the discourse. Speaking with Andreas, artistic director Alberto Barbera once again picked Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine as an early awards frontrunner, as buzz swept across the Lido. The longtime Venice chief also name-checked Lee Chang-Dong’s Possible Love and Robert Pattinson in Primetime as potential awards titles. Apart from the Oscars, Barbera also discussed the current AI race and much more. Read our full interview with him here. On the screenings side of things, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s NAZA landed a sensational 25-minute ovation following its world premiere on Thursday. That time sets a new record for any movie at a major festival, surpassing the near 24 minutes scored by The Voice of Hind Rajab at last year’s Venice. The documentary feature uncovers the Israeli military’s systematic killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Elsewhere, Florian Zeller’s latest Bunker, starring Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem, earned a 16-minute ovation. Alex Gibney’s Elon Musk doc was another thrilling the Venice audience. In his review, Deadline’s Matt Carey wrote: “Alex Gibney has made a lot of vital documentaries. This is his most important.” The explosive feature very much upset the world’s richest person, who called Gibney “a bitter old man.” Venice ends tomorrow. Follow our coverage of the closing night awards ceremony here. Over in Toronto, where things are just getting started, we’ve got a raft of reviews and plenty of news and package scoops for you to peruse, along with this great preview from Anthony D’Alessandro.

Watch on Deadline

The Deadline Interview: Mercedes Ron

Mercedes Ron; ‘Culpa Mía’ (My Fault) Diego Lafuente

Mercedes Ron has plenty to feel good about. The author is behind one of the biggest young adult film franchises of the past few years in Prime Video’s Culpables trilogy. As the first Latina author with a first-look Amazon MGM Studios deal, she’s now having ten of her Wattpad novels turned into feature films. Her new movie, Drawn Together, debuted on Wednesday, so Diana took the chance to sit down with her to talk about going from a 19-year-old with big dreams to one of international streaming’s most valuable creatives less than 15 years later. >>>International Disruptor

Royal Briefing Battle

Family feud: They’re barely back in the UK, but Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are already embroiled in a renewed family squabble. At the top of the week, Buckingham Palace preemptively put out a statement on behalf of King Charles III reminding the public that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are “no longer working members of the Royal Family.” The Sussexes then coordinated a media briefing to express “surprise” at the statement, only for Buckingham Palace to claim they had been made aware of its existence before it went wide. With Harry angry at his father and the establishment over a lack of security provision for his family, I can’t see a reunion on the cards just yet.

The Essentials

🌶️ Hot One: Spanish Grammy winner Rosalía is in early talks to join Alma Har’el’s buzzy TIFF market-bound family drama Wet.

🌶️ Another One: Netflix has picked up buzzy Australian documentary series 2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback globally ahead of its world premiere in Toronto.

🔥 And a Third: BBC Studios Fiction is developing The Paying Guests, the only Sarah Waters novel never to be adapted for screen, with Kayleigh Llewellyn attached to pen the script.

🤓 “Feisty one, you are!”: Netflix officially confirmed the Inbetweeners reunion movie, with Simon Bird, James Buckley, Blake Harrison and Joe Thomas reprising their roles.
